\NeedsTeXFormat{LaTeX2e}
\ProvidesClass{iopart}[1996/06/10 v0.0 IOP Journals LaTeX article class]
\newcommand\@ptsize{0}
\newif\if@restonecol
\newif\if@titlepage
\newif\ifiopams
\@titlepagefalse
\DeclareOption{a4paper}
   {\setlength\paperheight {297mm}%
    \setlength\paperwidth  {210mm}}
\DeclareOption{letterpaper}
   {\setlength\paperheight {11in}%
    \setlength\paperwidth  {8.5in}}
\DeclareOption{landscape}
   {\setlength\@tempdima   {\paperheight}%
    \setlength\paperheight {\paperwidth}%
    \setlength\paperwidth  {\@tempdima}}
\DeclareOption{10pt}{\renewcommand\@ptsize{0}}
\DeclareOption{11pt}{\renewcommand\@ptsize{2}} % No 11pt version
\DeclareOption{12pt}{\renewcommand\@ptsize{2}}
\DeclareOption{draft}{\setlength\overfullrule{5pt}}
\DeclareOption{final}{\setlength\overfullrule{0pt}}
\DeclareOption{titlepage}{\@titlepagetrue}
\DeclareOption{notitlepage}{\@titlepagefalse}
\ExecuteOptions{letterpaper,final}
\ProcessOptions
\DeclareMathAlphabet{\bi}{OML}{cmm}{b}{it}
\DeclareMathAlphabet{\bcal}{OMS}{cmsy}{b}{n}
\input{iopart1\@ptsize.clo}
\setlength\lineskip{1\p@}
\setlength\normallineskip{1\p@}
\renewcommand\baselinestretch{}

\@lowpenalty   51
\@medpenalty  151
\@highpenalty 301
\setlength\parindent{2em}
\setcounter{topnumber}{8}
\renewcommand\topfraction{1}
\setcounter{bottomnumber}{3}
\renewcommand\bottomfraction{.99}
\setcounter{totalnumber}{8}
\renewcommand\textfraction{0.01}

%
\pretolerance=5000
\tolerance=8000
%
% Headings for all pages apart from first
%
\def\ps@headings{\let\@oddfoot\@empty
      \let\@evenfoot\@empty
      \def\@evenhead{\thepage\hfil\itshape\rightmark}%
      \def\@oddhead{{\itshape\leftmark}\hfil\thepage}%
      \let\@mkboth\markboth
      \let\sectionmark\@gobble
      \let\subsectionmark\@gobble}
%
% Headings for first page
%
\def\ps@myheadings{\let\@oddfoot\@empty\let\@evenfoot\@empty
    \let\@oddhead\@empty\let\@evenhead\@empty
    \let\@mkboth\@gobbletwo
    \let\sectionmark\@gobble
    \let\subsectionmark\@gobble}
%
% \maketitle just ends page
%
\newcommand\maketitle{\newpage}
%
% Article titles
%
% Usage: \title[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\renewcommand{\title}{\@ifnextchar[{\@stitle}{\@ftitle}}
\def\@stitle[#1]#2{\markboth{#1}{#1}%
    \thispagestyle{myheadings}%
    \vspace*{3pc}{\exhyphenpenalty=10000\hyphenpenalty=10000 
    \Large\raggedright\noindent
    \bf#2\par}}
\def\@ftitle#1{\markboth{#1}{#1}%
    \thispagestyle{myheadings}%
    \vspace*{3pc}{\exhyphenpenalty=10000\hyphenpenalty=10000 
    \Large\raggedright\noindent
    \bf#1\par}}
%
% Can use \paper instead of \title
%
\let\paper=\title
%
% Generic title command for articles other than papers
%
% Usage: \article[Short title]{Article Type}{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\newcommand{\article}{\@ifnextchar[{\@sarticle}{\@farticle}}
\def\@sarticle[#1]#2#3{\markboth{#1}{#1}%
    \thispagestyle{myheadings}%
     \vspace*{.5pc}%
    {\parindent=\mathindent \bf #2\par}%
     \vspace*{1.5pc}%
    {\exhyphenpenalty=10000\hyphenpenalty=10000
     \Large\raggedright\noindent
     \bf#3\par}}%
\def\@farticle#1#2{\markboth{#2}{#2}%
    \thispagestyle{myheadings}%
     \vspace*{.5pc}%
    {\parindent=\mathindent \bf #1\par}%
     \vspace*{1.5pc}%
    {\exhyphenpenalty=10000\hyphenpenalty=10000
     \Large\raggedright\noindent
     \bf#2\par}}%
%
% Letters to the Editor
%
% Usage \letter{Full title}
% No short title is required for Letters
%
\def\letter#1{\article[Letter to the Editor]{Letter to the Editor}{#1}}
%
% Fast Track Communications (added by sxb 9 March 2011)
%
% Usage \ftc{Full title} - there's no short title
\def\ftc#1{\article[Fast Track Communication]{Fast Track Communication}{#1}}
%
%
% Review articles
%
% Usage: \review[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\review{\@ifnextchar[{\@sreview}{\@freview}}
\def\@sreview[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Review Article}{#2}}
\def\@freview#1{\@farticle{Review Article}{#1}}
%
% Topical Review
%
% Usage: \topical[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\topical{\@ifnextchar[{\@stopical}{\@ftopical}}
\def\@stopical[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Topical Review}{#2}}
\def\@ftopical#1{\@farticle{Topical Review}{#1}}
%
% Comments
%
% Usage: \comment[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\comment{\@ifnextchar[{\@scomment}{\@fcomment}}
\def\@scomment[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Comment}{#2}}
\def\@fcomment#1{\@farticle{Comment}{#1}}
%
% Rapid Communications
%
% Usage: \rapid[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\rapid{\@ifnextchar[{\@srapid}{\@frapid}}
\def\@srapid[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Rapid Communication}{#2}}
\def\@frapid#1{\@farticle{Rapid Communication}{#1}}
%
% Notes
%
% Usage: \note[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\note{\@ifnextchar[{\@snote}{\@fnote}}
\def\@snote[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Note}{#2}}
\def\@fnote#1{\@farticle{Note}{#1}}
%
% Preliminary Communications
%
% Usage: \prelim[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\prelim{\@ifnextchar[{\@sprelim}{\@fprelim}}
\def\@sprelim[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Preliminary Communication}{#2}}
\def\@fprelim#1{\@farticle{Preliminary Communication}{#1}}
%
% List of authors
%
% Usage \author[Short form]{List of all authors}
% The short form excludes footnote symbols linking authors to addresses 
% and is used for running heads in printed version (but not on preprints)
%
\renewcommand{\author}{\@ifnextchar[{\@sauthor}{\@fauthor}}
\def\@sauthor[#1]#2{\markright{#1}    % for production only
   \vspace*{1.5pc}%
   \begin{indented}%
   \item[]\normalsize\bf\raggedright#2
   \end{indented}%
   \smallskip}
\def\@fauthor#1{%\markright{#1}         for production only
   \vspace*{1.5pc}%
   \begin{indented}%
   \item[]\normalsize\bf\raggedright#1
   \end{indented}%
   \smallskip}
%
% Affiliation (authors address)
%
% Usage: \address{Address of first author}
%        \address{Address of second author}
% Use once for each address, use symbols \dag \ddag \S \P $\|$
% to connect authors with addresses
%
\newcommand{\address}[1]{\begin{indented}
   \item[]\rm\raggedright #1
   \end{indented}}
%
% American Mathematical Society Classification Numbers
% Usage: \ams{57.XX, 58.XX}
%
\def\ams#1{\vspace{10pt}
     \begin{indented}
     \item[]\rm AMS classification scheme numbers: #1\par
     \end{indented}}
%
% A single Physics & Astronomy Classification Number
% Usage \pacno{31.10}
%
\def\pacno#1{\vspace{10pt}
     \begin{indented}
     \item[]\rm PACS number: #1\par
     \end{indented}}
%
% Physics & Astronomy Classification Numbers (more than one)
% Usage \pacs{31.10, 31.20T}
%
\def\pacs#1{\vspace{10pt}
     \begin{indented}
     \item[]\rm PACS numbers: #1\par
     \end{indented}}
%
% Submission details. If \jl command used journals name printed
% otherwise Institute of Physics Publishing 
%
\def\submitted{\vspace{28pt plus 10pt minus 18pt}
     \noindent{\small\rm Submitted to: {\it \journal}\par}}
%
\def\submitto#1{\vspace{28pt plus 10pt minus 18pt}
     \noindent{\small\rm Submitted to: {\it #1}\par}}
%
% For articles (other than Letters) not divided into sections
% Usage \nosections Start of text
%
\def\nosections{\vspace{30\p@ plus12\p@ minus12\p@}
    \noindent\ignorespaces}
%
% Acknowledgments (no heading if letter)
% Usage \ack for Acknowledgments, \ackn for Acknowledgement
%
\def\ack{\ifletter\bigskip\noindent\ignorespaces\else
    \section*{Acknowledgments}\fi}
\def\ackn{\ifletter\bigskip\noindent\ignorespaces\else
    \section*{Acknowledgment}\fi}
%
% Footnotes: symbols selected in order \dag (1), \ddag (2), \S (3), 
% $\|$ (4), $\P$ (5), $^+$ (6), $^*$ (7), \sharp (8), \dagger\dagger (9)
% unless optional argument of [<num>] use to specify required symbol, 
% 1=\dag, 2=\ddag, etc
% Usage: \footnote{Text of footnote}
%        \footnote[3]{Text of footnote}
%
\def\footnoterule{}%
\setcounter{footnote}{1}
\long\def\@makefntext#1{\parindent 1em\noindent 
 \makebox[1em][l]{\footnotesize\rm$\m@th{\fnsymbol{footnote}}$}%
 \footnotesize\rm #1}
\def\@makefnmark{\hbox{${\fnsymbol{footnote}}\m@th$}}
\def\@thefnmark{\fnsymbol{footnote}}
\def\footnote{\@ifnextchar[{\@xfootnote}{\stepcounter{\@mpfn}%
       \begingroup\let\protect\noexpand
       \xdef\@thefnmark{\thempfn}\endgroup
     \@footnotemark\@footnotetext}}
\def\@xfootnote[#1]{\setcounter{footnote}{#1}%
   \addtocounter{footnote}{-1}\footnote}
\def\@fnsymbol#1{\ifcase#1\or \dagger\or \ddagger\or \S\or
   \|\or \P\or ^{+}\or ^{\tsty *}\or \sharp
   \or \dagger\dagger \else\@ctrerr\fi\relax}

%
% E-mail addresses (to provide links from headers)
%
\def\eads#1{\vspace*{5pt}\address{E-mail: #1}}
\def\ead#1{\vspace*{5pt}\address{E-mail: \mailto{#1}}}
\def\mailto#1{{\tt #1}}
%
% Switches
%
\newif\ifletter
%
\setcounter{secnumdepth}{3}
\newcounter {section}
\newcounter {subsection}[section]
\newcounter {subsubsection}[subsection]
\newcounter {paragraph}[subsubsection]
\newcounter {subparagraph}[paragraph]
\renewcommand\thesection       {\arabic{section}}
\renewcommand\thesubsection    {\thesection.\arabic{subsection}}
\renewcommand\thesubsubsection {\thesubsection.\arabic{subsubsection}}
\renewcommand\theparagraph     {\thesubsubsection.\arabic{paragraph}}
\renewcommand\thesubparagraph  {\theparagraph.\arabic{subparagraph}}
\def\@chapapp{Section}

\newcommand\section{\@startsection {section}{1}{\z@}%
                   {-3.5ex \@plus -1ex \@minus -.2ex}%
                   {2.3ex \@plus.2ex}%
                   {\reset@font\normalsize\bfseries\raggedright}}
\newcommand\subsection{\@startsection{subsection}{2}{\z@}%
                   {-3.25ex\@plus -1ex \@minus -.2ex}%
                   {1.5ex \@plus .2ex}%
                   {\reset@font\normalsize\itshape\raggedright}}
\newcommand\subsubsection{\@startsection{subsubsection}{3}{\z@}%
                                     {-3.25ex\@plus -1ex \@minus -.2ex}%
                                     {-1em \@plus .2em}%
                                     {\reset@font\normalsize\itshape}}
\newcommand\paragraph{\@startsection{paragraph}{4}{\z@}%
                                    {3.25ex \@plus1ex \@minus.2ex}%
                                    {-1em}%
                                    {\reset@font\normalsize\itshape}}
\newcommand\subparagraph{\@startsection{subparagraph}{5}{\parindent}%
                                       {3.25ex \@plus1ex \@minus .2ex}%
                                       {-1em}%
                                      {\reset@font\normalsize\itshape}}
\def\@sect#1#2#3#4#5#6[#7]#8{\ifnum #2>\c@secnumdepth
     \let\@svsec\@empty\else
     \refstepcounter{#1}\edef\@svsec{\csname the#1\endcsname. }\fi
     \@tempskipa #5\relax
      \ifdim \@tempskipa>\z@
        \begingroup #6\relax
          \noindent{\hskip #3\relax\@svsec}{\interlinepenalty \@M #8\par}%
        \endgroup
       \csname #1mark\endcsname{#7}\addcontentsline
         {toc}{#1}{\ifnum #2>\c@secnumdepth \else
                      \protect\numberline{\csname the#1\endcsname}\fi
                    #7}\else
        \def\@svsechd{#6\hskip #3\relax  %% \relax added 2 May 90
                   \@svsec #8\csname #1mark\endcsname
                      {#7}\addcontentsline
                           {toc}{#1}{\ifnum #2>\c@secnumdepth \else
                             \protect\numberline{\csname the#1\endcsname}\fi
                       #7}}\fi
     \@xsect{#5}}
%
\def\@ssect#1#2#3#4#5{\@tempskipa #3\relax
   \ifdim \@tempskipa>\z@
     \begingroup #4\noindent{\hskip #1}{\interlinepenalty \@M #5\par}\endgroup
   \else \def\@svsechd{#4\hskip #1\relax #5}\fi
    \@xsect{#3}}

\renewcommand\theenumi{\roman{enumi}}

\renewcommand\theenumiii{\arabic{enumiii}}

\newcommand\labelenumii{(\theenumii)}
\newcommand\labelenumiii{\theenumiii.}
\newcommand\labelenumiv{(\theenumiv)}

\renewcommand\p@enumiii{(\theenumi.\theenumii)}

\newenvironment{description}
               {\list{}{\labelwidth\z@ \itemindent-\leftmargin
                        \let\makelabel\descriptionlabel}}
               {\endlist}
\newcommand\descriptionlabel[1]{\hspace\labelsep
                                \normalfont\bfseries #1}
\newenvironment{abstract}{%
      \vspace{16pt plus3pt minus3pt}
      \begin{indented}
      \item[]{\bfseries \abstractname.}\quad\rm\ignorespaces} 
      {\end{indented}\if@titlepage\newpage\else\vspace{18\p@ plus18\p@}\fi}
\newenvironment{verse}
               {\let\\=\@centercr
                \list{}{\itemsep      \z@
                        \itemindent   -1.5em%
                        \listparindent\itemindent
                        \rightmargin  \leftmargin
                        \advance\leftmargin 1.5em}%
                \item[]}
               {\endlist}
\newenvironment{quotation}
               {\list{}{\listparindent 1.5em%
                        \itemindent    \listparindent
                        \rightmargin   \leftmargin
                        \parsep        \z@ \@plus\p@}%
                \item[]}
               {\endlist}
\newenvironment{quote}
               {\list{}{\rightmargin\leftmargin}%
                \item[]}
               {\endlist}
\newenvironment{titlepage}
    {%
        \@restonecolfalse\newpage
      \thispagestyle{empty}%
      \if@compatibility
        \setcounter{page}{0}
      \else
        \setcounter{page}{1}%
      \fi}%
    {\newpage\setcounter{page}{1}}
\def\appendix{\@ifnextchar*{\@appendixstar}{\@appendix}}
\def\@appendix{\eqnobysec\@appendixstar}
\def\@appendixstar{\@@par
 \ifnumbysec                         %  Added 30/4/94 to get Table A1,
 \@addtoreset{table}{section}        %  Table B1 etc if numbering by
 \@addtoreset{figure}{section}\fi    %  section
 \setcounter{section}{0}
 \setcounter{subsection}{0}
 \setcounter{subsubsection}{0}
 \setcounter{equation}{0}
 \setcounter{figure}{0}
 \setcounter{table}{0}
 \def\thesection{Appendix \Alph{section}}   
 \def\theequation{\ifnumbysec
      \Alph{section}.\arabic{equation}\else
      \Alph{section}\arabic{equation}\fi}  % Comment A\arabic{equation} maybe
 \def\thetable{\ifnumbysec                 % better? 15/4/95
      \Alph{section}\arabic{table}\else
      A\arabic{table}\fi}
 \def\thefigure{\ifnumbysec
      \Alph{section}\arabic{figure}\else
      A\arabic{figure}\fi}}
\def\noappendix{\setcounter{figure}{0}
     \setcounter{table}{0}
     \def\thetable{\arabic{table}}
     \def\thefigure{\arabic{figure}}}

%
% Added redefinition of \@caption so captions are not written to 
% aux file therefore less need to \protect fragile commands
%
\long\def\@caption#1[#2]#3{\par\begingroup
    \@parboxrestore
    \normalsize
    \@makecaption{\csname fnum@#1\endcsname}{\ignorespaces #3}\par
  \endgroup}
% 
\long\def\@makecaption#1#2{\vskip \abovecaptionskip 
 \begin{indented}
 \item[]{\bf #1.} #2
 \end{indented}\vskip\belowcaptionskip}
\let\@portraitcaption=\@makecaption

\newcommand\@pnumwidth{1.55em}
\newcommand\@tocrmarg {2.55em}
\newcommand\@dotsep{4.5}
\setcounter{tocdepth}{3}
\newcommand\tableofcontents{%
    \section*{\contentsname
        \@mkboth{\uppercase{\contentsname}}{\uppercase{\contentsname}}}%
    \@starttoc{toc}%
    }
\newcommand\l@part[2]{%
  \ifnum \c@tocdepth >-2\relax
    \addpenalty{\@secpenalty}%
    \addvspace{2.25em \@plus\p@}%
    \begingroup
      \setlength\@tempdima{3em}%
      \parindent \z@ \rightskip \@pnumwidth
      \parfillskip -\@pnumwidth
      {\leavevmode
       \large \bfseries #1\hfil \hbox to\@pnumwidth{\hss #2}}\par
       \nobreak
       \if@compatibility
         \global\@nobreaktrue
         \everypar{\global\@nobreakfalse\everypar{}}
      \fi
    \endgroup
  \fi}
\newcommand\l@section[2]{%
  \ifnum \c@tocdepth >\z@
    \addpenalty{\@secpenalty}%
    \addvspace{1.0em \@plus\p@}%
    \setlength\@tempdima{1.5em}%
    \begingroup
      \parindent \z@ \rightskip \@pnumwidth
      \parfillskip -\@pnumwidth
      \leavevmode \bfseries
      \advance\leftskip\@tempdima
      \hskip -\leftskip
      #1\nobreak\hfil \nobreak\hbox to\@pnumwidth{\hss #2}\par
    \endgroup
  \fi}
\newcommand\l@subsection   {\@dottedtocline{2}{1.5em}{2.3em}}
\newcommand\l@subsubsection{\@dottedtocline{3}{3.8em}{3.2em}}
\newcommand\l@paragraph    {\@dottedtocline{4}{7.0em}{4.1em}}
\newcommand\l@subparagraph {\@dottedtocline{5}{10em}{5em}}
\newcommand\listoffigures{%
    \section*{\listfigurename
      \@mkboth{\uppercase{\listfigurename}}%
              {\uppercase{\listfigurename}}}%
    \@starttoc{lof}%
    }
\newcommand\l@figure{\@dottedtocline{1}{1.5em}{2.3em}}
\newcommand\listoftables{%
    \section*{\listtablename
      \@mkboth{\uppercase{\listtablename}}{\uppercase{\listtablename}}}%
    \@starttoc{lot}%
    }
\let\l@table\l@figure
\newenvironment{theindex}
               {\if@twocolumn
                  \@restonecolfalse
                \else
                  \@restonecoltrue
                \fi
                \columnseprule \z@
                \columnsep 35\p@
                \twocolumn[\section*{\indexname}]%
                \@mkboth{\uppercase{\indexname}}%
                        {\uppercase{\indexname}}%
                \thispagestyle{plain}\parindent\z@
                \parskip\z@ \@plus .3\p@\relax
                \let\item\@idxitem}
               {\if@restonecol\onecolumn\else\clearpage\fi}
\newcommand\@idxitem  {\par\hangindent 40\p@}
\newcommand\subitem   {\par\hangindent 40\p@ \hspace*{20\p@}}
\newcommand\subsubitem{\par\hangindent 40\p@ \hspace*{30\p@}}
\newcommand\indexspace{\par \vskip 10\p@ \@plus5\p@ \@minus3\p@\relax}
\newcommand\contentsname{Contents}
\newcommand\listfigurename{List of Figures}
\newcommand\listtablename{List of Tables}
\newcommand\refname{References}
\newcommand\indexname{Index}
\newcommand\figurename{Figure}
\newcommand\tablename{Table}
\newcommand\partname{Part}
\newcommand\appendixname{Appendix}
\newcommand\abstractname{Abstract}

  January\or February\or March\or April\or May\or June\or
  July\or August\or September\or October\or November\or December\fi
  \space\number\year}

    \def\fps@table{hp}\noappendix}
\newcommand{\Figures}{\clearpage\section*{Figure captions}
    \def\fps@figure{hp}\noappendix}

\newcommand{\Figure}[1]{\begin{figure}
  \caption{#1}
  \end{figure}}
%
\newcommand{\Table}[1]{\begin{table}
  \caption{#1}
  \begin{indented}
  \lineup
  \item[]\begin{tabular}{@{}l*{15}{l}}}

\def\endTable{\end{tabular}\end{indented}\end{table}}
\let\endtab=\endTable
%
\newcommand{\fulltable}[1]{\begin{table}
  \caption{#1}
  \footnotesize
  \lineup
  \begin{tabular*}{\textwidth}{@{}l*{15}{@{\extracolsep{0pt plus 12pt}}l}}}
\def\endfulltable{\end{tabular*}\end{table}\normalsize}

%
\newcommand{\Bibliography}[1]{\section*{References}\par\numrefs{#1}}
\newcommand{\References}{\section*{References}\par\refs}

\def\thebibliography#1{\list
 {\hfil[\arabic{enumi}]}{\topsep=0\p@\parsep=0\p@
 \partopsep=0\p@\itemsep=0\p@
 \labelsep=5\p@\itemindent=-10\p@
 \settowidth\labelwidth{\footnotesize[#1]}%
 \leftmargin\labelwidth
 \advance\leftmargin\labelsep
 \advance\leftmargin -\itemindent
 \usecounter{enumi}}\footnotesize
 \def\newblock{\ }
 \sloppy\clubpenalty4000\widowpenalty4000
 \sfcode`\.=1000\relax}
\let\endthebibliography=\endlist
\def\numrefs#1{\begin{thebibliography}{#1}}
\def\endnumrefs{\end{thebibliography}}
\let\endbib=\endnumrefs
%
\def\thereferences{\list{}{\topsep=0\p@\parsep=0\p@
 \partopsep=0\p@\itemsep=0\p@\labelsep=0\p@\itemindent=-18\p@
\labelwidth=0\p@\leftmargin=18\p@
}\footnotesize\rm
\def\newblock{\ }
\sloppy\clubpenalty4000\widowpenalty4000
\sfcode`\.=1000\relax
}
%
\let\endthereferences=\endlist
\newlength{\indentedwidth}
\newdimen\mathindent
\indentedwidth=\mathindent
%
% Macro to used for references in the Harvard system
%
\newenvironment{harvard}{\list{}{\topsep=0\p@\parsep=0\p@
\partopsep=0\p@\itemsep=0\p@\labelsep=0\p@\itemindent=-18\p@
\labelwidth=0\p@\leftmargin=18\p@
}\footnotesize\rm
\def\newblock{\ }
\sloppy\clubpenalty4000\widowpenalty4000
\sfcode`\.=1000\relax}{\endlist}
%
\def\refs{\begin{harvard}}
\def\endrefs{\end{harvard}}
%
\newenvironment{indented}{\begin{indented}}{\end{indented}}
\newenvironment{varindent}[1]{\begin{varindent}{#1}}{\end{varindent}}
%
\def\indented{\list{}{\itemsep=0\p@\labelsep=0\p@\itemindent=0\p@
   \labelwidth=0\p@\leftmargin=\mathindent\topsep=0\p@\partopsep=0\p@
   \parsep=0\p@\listparindent=15\p@}\footnotesize\rm}

\let\endindented=\endlist 

\def\varindent#1{\setlength{\varind}{#1}%
   \list{}{\itemsep=0\p@\labelsep=0\p@\itemindent=0\p@
   \labelwidth=0\p@\leftmargin=\varind\topsep=0\p@\partopsep=0\p@
   \parsep=0\p@\listparindent=15\p@}\footnotesize\rm}

\let\endvarindent=\endlist 

\def\[{\relax\ifmmode\@badmath\else
 \begin{trivlist}
 \@beginparpenalty\predisplaypenalty
 \@endparpenalty\postdisplaypenalty
 \item[]\leavevmode
 \hbox to\linewidth\bgroup$ \displaystyle
 \hskip\mathindent\bgroup\fi}
\def\]{\relax\ifmmode \egroup $\hfil \egroup \end{trivlist}\else \@badmath \fi}
\def\equation{\@beginparpenalty\predisplaypenalty
 \@endparpenalty\postdisplaypenalty
\refstepcounter{equation}\trivlist \item[]\leavevmode
 \hbox to\linewidth\bgroup $ \displaystyle
\hskip\mathindent}
\def\endequation{$\hfil \displaywidth\linewidth\@eqnnum\egroup \endtrivlist}
%
\@namedef{equation*}{\[}
\@namedef{endequation*}{\]}
%
\def\eqnarray{\stepcounter{equation}\let\@currentlabel=\theequation
\global\@eqnswtrue
\global\@eqcnt\z@\tabskip\mathindent\let\\=\@eqncr
\abovedisplayskip\topsep\ifvmode\advance\abovedisplayskip\partopsep\fi
\belowdisplayskip\abovedisplayskip
\belowdisplayshortskip\abovedisplayskip
\abovedisplayshortskip\abovedisplayskip
$$\halign to
\linewidth\bgroup\@eqnsel$\displaystyle\tabskip\z@
 {##{}}$&\global\@eqcnt\@ne $\displaystyle{{}##{}}$\hfil
 &\global\@eqcnt\tw@ $\displaystyle{{}##}$\hfil
 \tabskip\@centering&\llap{##}\tabskip\z@\cr}
\def\endeqnarray{\@@eqncr\egroup
 \global\advance\c@equation\m@ne$$\global\@ignoretrue }
\mathindent = 6pc
%
\def\eqalign#1{\null\vcenter{\def\\{\cr}\openup\jot\m@th
  \ialign{\strut$\displaystyle{##}$\hfil&$\displaystyle{{}##}$\hfil
      \crcr#1\crcr}}\,}
%
\def\eqalignno#1{\displ@y \tabskip\z@skip
  \halign to\displaywidth{\hspace{5pc}$\@lign\displaystyle{##}$%
    \tabskip\z@skip
    &$\@lign\displaystyle{{}##}$\hfill\tabskip\@centering
    &\llap{$\@lign\hbox{\rm##}$}\tabskip\z@skip\crcr
    #1\crcr}}
%
\newif\ifnumbysec
\def\theequation{\ifnumbysec
      \arabic{section}.\arabic{equation}\else
      \arabic{equation}\fi}
\def\eqnobysec{\numbysectrue\@addtoreset{equation}{section}}

\newcounter{eqnval}

% 2012: if you have an eqn numbered by parts (eg eqn 6a, 6b) this allows
% you to refer to it by just the number (eg eqn 6) if the label is between
% the \multiparteqn and the \numparts
\def\multiparteqn{\addtocounter{equation}{1}
\eqnarray\nonumber
\endeqnarray

\vspace{-72pt}
}

\def\numparts{\addtocounter{equation}{1}%
     \setcounter{eqnval}{\value{equation}}%
     \setcounter{equation}{0}%
     \def\theequation{\ifnumbysec
     \arabic{section}.\arabic{eqnval}{\it\alph{equation}}%
     \else\arabic{eqnval}{\it\alph{equation}}\fi}}

\def\endnumparts{\def\theequation{\ifnumbysec
     \arabic{section}.\arabic{equation}\else
     \arabic{equation}\fi}%
     \setcounter{equation}{\value{eqnval}}}
%
\def\cases#1{%
     \left\{\,\vcenter{\def\\{\cr}\normalbaselines\openup1\jot\m@th%
     \ialign{\strut$\displaystyle{##}\hfil$&\tqs
     \rm##\hfil\crcr#1\crcr}}\right.}%

\newcommand\small{%
   \@setfontsize\small\@ixpt{11}%
   \abovedisplayskip 8.5\p@ \@plus3\p@ \@minus4\p@
   \abovedisplayshortskip \z@ \@plus2\p@

\title[The Foundation of Calculus]{The Foundation of Calculus: Limits, Local Change and Accumulation}
\author{Sohel Georgiadis}
\address{Student, The Reality Public School\\Kokrajhar, Assam, India}
\ead{\href{mailto:sohelgeorgiadis@gmail.com}{sohelgeorgiadis@gmail.com}}
\vspace{10pt}
\begin{indented}\item[]25 April 2026\end{indented}
\begin{abstract}
This exposition develops single-variable calculus through the control of approximation error. Completeness supplies limits, differentiation identifies a local linear model, and Riemann integration defines accumulation through partitions. The Mean Value Theorem connects pointwise derivative information with finite change. The Fundamental Theorem then relates the accumulation function to its integrand and yields endpoint evaluation. These results support optimisation, Newton iteration, logarithms and exponentials, integration techniques, geometric applications, and parametric and polar curves. Improper integrals and infinite series are treated as limit problems with explicit convergence conditions. Taylor approximation is separated from representation by an infinite series, with a smooth nonanalytic function showing why the remainder cannot be discarded. Reproducible calculations examine finite-difference error, quadrature convergence and root finding. An advanced appendix uses a sampled Newton basin image for a cubic polynomial to illustrate the global sensitivity of iteration, with its finite grid, stopping tolerance and iteration cap retained as part of the interpretation. The real-number completeness axiom and several compactness consequences are stated explicitly. The results concern established mathematics and numerical illustrations; the images and computations do not replace proofs.
\end{abstract}
\vspace{-6pt}

\section{Introduction and scope}

A tangent line and an accumulated area appear to ask for different information. The tangent describes behaviour near one point. The area records contributions across an interval. Calculus connects them by making both constructions depend on a limit whose error can be controlled. The connection is strongest when the hypotheses are kept visible. A drawing can suggest a tangent, but a corner can prevent its slope from existing. A sequence of finer sums can suggest an area, but a bounded function need not be Riemann integrable.

The central problem here is to determine when a local approximation gives reliable information about a finite change or an accumulated total. Differentiation supplies a linear approximation with an error smaller than its input increment. The Mean Value Theorem turns this local information into a statement across an interval. Integration then asks whether the errors made in replacing a function by many simple pieces disappear together. The Fundamental Theorem explains why these two operations meet.

The same concern persists when the calculations become more elaborate. An integration substitution must account for how intervals change. An infinite series needs a limit of partial sums. A Taylor polynomial needs a remainder estimate. Newton's method can be extremely accurate near a suitable root while behaving poorly elsewhere. None of these distinctions is visible from a formula alone.

The prerequisites are algebra, elementary functions, plane geometry, trigonometry and the arithmetic of inequalities. Limits and one-variable derivatives and integrals are developed within the exposition. The ordered-field properties and completeness of $\R$ are assumed. Several consequences of compactness are stated with their roles identified rather than replaced by a construction of the real numbers. The standard real-variable development ends with the conclusions. \ref{sec:basins} is an optional advanced extension to Newton dynamics in the complex plane. It introduces the complex arithmetic needed to iterate a polynomial and does not form part of the prerequisites for the main text.

The source courses supply complementary viewpoints. The main single-variable course provides the computational range. The revisited course sharpens the interpretation of limiting operations. The visual lessons motivate local change and accumulation, while the real-analysis lectures provide precise hypotheses and counterexamples. Source attribution and a guide to the downloaded transcript archive appear in the bibliography. The development here is a connected exposition rather than a sequence of lecture summaries.

\subsection{Notation and the status of an approximation}

The independent variable is usually $x$. An increment $h$ is a nonzero real number that may have either sign. The notation $h\to0$ describes a limiting process; it does not give $h$ the value zero inside a quotient. A limit is evaluated within the domain of the function. Unless specified otherwise, an interval is a real interval and angles are measured in radians.

We write $r(h)=o(h)$ when $r(h)/h\to0$. We write $r(h)=O(h^p)$ near zero if $|r(h)|\leq C|h|^p$ there for some constant $C$ independent of $h$. The first notation expresses a vanishing relative error; the second gives a bound on its size. Neither notation by itself identifies the numerical value of the error.

\eqdisplay{r(h)=o(h)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \lim_{h\to0}\frac{r(h)}h=0,\qquad |r(h)|\leq C|h|^p\ \Longrightarrow\ r(h)=O(h^p).}

An exact equality, an asymptotic statement and a computed decimal have different meanings. These distinctions will be retained even when their graphs look indistinguishable at the displayed scale.

\FloatBarrier
\section{Real numbers and completeness}

\subsection{An ordered field does not yet supply every limit}

Rational arithmetic permits addition, multiplication and division by nonzero numbers. It also permits order comparisons. Yet a rational sequence can approach a number absent from the rationals. To see the obstruction without relying on a decimal picture, suppose $\sqrt2=p/q$ for coprime integers $p,q>0$. Then $p^2=2q^2$, so $p$ is even. Writing $p=2k$ gives $q^2=2k^2$, so $q$ is also even. This contradicts coprimality.

The calculation does not say that the equation $x^2=2$ has no real solution. It says that rational arithmetic alone has a gap relevant to a limiting construction. Calculus needs a number system in which suitable approximations can have limits within the system.

An upper bound of a set $S$ is a number $b$ with $s\leq b$ for every $s\in S$. Its least upper bound, written $\sup S$, is the smallest such number. Completeness asserts that every nonempty subset of $\R$ bounded above has a real least upper bound. This is an axiom of the real-number model used here. It is not being proved from a picture of the number line.

\subsection{Monotone approximation}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded monotone convergence]\label{thm:monotone}
Every increasing real sequence bounded above converges to the supremum of its terms. Every decreasing real sequence bounded below also converges.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $(a_n)$ be increasing and bounded above, and let $L=\sup\{a_n:n\in\N\}$. For any $\epsilon>0$, the number $L-\epsilon$ cannot be an upper bound. Some $a_N$ therefore exceeds it. Monotonicity gives, for every $n\geq N$,

\eqdisplay{L-\epsilon<a_N\leq a_n\leq L,\qquad |a_n-L|<\epsilon.}

Thus an increasing bounded sequence converges. A decreasing bounded sequence follows by changing signs. The proof identifies where completeness enters: it supplies $L$ before the approximation argument begins.
\end{proof}

For $0<q<1$, the geometric partial sums are increasing and bounded. Their finite algebraic identity also gives the error explicitly:

\eqdisplay{\sum_{k=0}^n q^k=\frac{1-q^{n+1}}{1-q},\qquad \frac1{1-q}-\sum_{k=0}^nq^k=\frac{q^{n+1}}{1-q}.}

The right-hand error tends to zero. This conclusion concerns a sequence of finite sums. It does not require performing infinitely many additions as a completed arithmetic procedure.

\subsection{Cauchy sequences and interval consequences}

A sequence is Cauchy if its sufficiently late terms are as close to one another as any prescribed tolerance requires:

\eqdisplay{\forall\epsilon>0\ \exists N\ \forall m,n\geq N:\quad |a_n-a_m|<\epsilon.}

Every convergent sequence is Cauchy by the triangle inequality. The converse holds in $\R$ and is an equivalent form of completeness. In $\mathbb Q$ the converse can fail, because the approximations may approach a missing irrational value. We use the real Cauchy convergence theorem as an established consequence of the least-upper-bound axiom.

Three further consequences will be needed. A continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains a maximum and minimum, takes every intermediate value, and is uniformly continuous there. Their proofs can be organised using convergent subsequences or nested intervals. The derivative and integration arguments below will state exactly where these interval theorems are used.

The closed and bounded qualification matters. The function $1/x$ is continuous on $(0,1)$ but is unbounded, while $x$ on $(0,1)$ has neither a largest nor a smallest value. Continuity at each individual point cannot supply missing endpoints or control an unbounded domain.

\FloatBarrier
\section{Limits and continuity}

\subsection{The order of the quantifiers}

To say that $f(x)$ tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $a$ is to require that every output tolerance can be met by restricting the input sufficiently. The point $a$ must be an accumulation point of the domain, so there are domain points arbitrarily near it other than itself. The definition is

\eqdisplay{\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall\epsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0:\ 0<|x-a|<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x)-L|<\epsilon.}

The chosen $\delta$ may depend on $\epsilon$ and $a$, but it must work for every admissible $x$ in that neighbourhood. Choosing a new $\delta$ after seeing each individual $x$ would not establish the stated limit. The puncture $0<|x-a|$ separates nearby behaviour from the value assigned at $a$.

\begin{example}[An explicit tolerance bound]
For $f(x)=x^2$ at $a=2$, factor the error. First impose $|x-2|<1$, so $|x+2|<5$. Then

\eqdisplay{|x^2-4|=|x-2||x+2|<5|x-2|,\qquad \delta=\min\{1,\epsilon/5\}.}

This single choice proves the limit for every positive $\epsilon$. It is a sufficient neighbourhood, not necessarily the largest possible one. A proof needs a working bound, not the optimal bound.
\end{example}

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calc-01-limits.pdf}
\caption{Calculated limit examples. Left: $(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ for $x\ne1$, with the value at 1 deliberately assigned to be 1. The limit is still 2. Right: an input neighbourhood guaranteeing the displayed output tolerance for $x^2$ at 2. The graphs illustrate the definitions; the bounds in the text establish them.}\label{fig:limits}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Uniqueness and the rules for combining limits}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness of a finite limit]
A function has at most one finite limit at any accumulation point of its domain.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $L\ne M$, choose tolerance $|L-M|/3$ around each proposed limit and restrict to a common neighbourhood. The triangle inequality would give

\eqdisplay{|L-M|\leq |L-f(x)|+|f(x)-M|<\frac23|L-M|,}

which is impossible. Nearby domain points exist by the accumulation-point assumption.
\end{proof}

If $f\to L$ and $g\to M$, the sum tends to $L+M$ because the two errors can each be bounded by half the desired tolerance. For the product, write

\eqdisplay{f(x)g(x)-LM=f(x)[g(x)-M]+M[f(x)-L].}

A function with a finite limit is bounded in some punctured neighbourhood. This bounds the factor $f(x)$, after which the two errors can again be controlled. Quotients are handled by keeping the denominator separated from zero; the condition is $M\ne0$. Substitution into a continuous outer function follows from applying its input tolerance to the inner function's output error.

The squeeze theorem uses order instead. If $u(x)\leq f(x)\leq v(x)$ near $a$, and both outer functions tend to $L$, their tolerance bounds trap $f$ in the same band. For example, $|x\sin(1/x)|\leq |x|$ proves a zero limit despite continued oscillation of the sine factor.

\subsection{A missing value, a jump and an unbounded limit}

For $x\ne1$, $(x^2-1)/(x-1)=x+1$. Its limit at 1 is 2, regardless of whether the original quotient is undefined there or a separate value is assigned. Defining the value to be 2 repairs the discontinuity. A jump cannot be repaired this way because its one-sided limits disagree.

One-sided limits restrict the approach to $x>a$ or $x<a$. A two-sided finite limit exists precisely when both one-sided limits exist and agree, for a domain containing a punctured interval. The function $|x|/x$ has right limit 1 and left limit $-1$ at zero. No assignment at zero reconciles them.

The notation $f(x)\to+\infty$ is a statement of unbounded growth, not convergence to a real number. For every $M>0$, a sufficiently small punctured neighbourhood must give $f(x)>M$. Thus $1/x^2\to+\infty$ at zero, while $1/x$ has opposite infinite one-sided limits. At infinity, the input condition is instead $x>A$ for sufficiently large $A$.

\subsection{Continuity and uniform continuity}

A function is continuous at $a$ when it is defined there and its limit there equals $f(a)$. In the tolerance definition the puncture can then be removed. Polynomials are continuous by the limit rules, and rational functions are continuous wherever their denominators are nonzero.

Continuity is local. Uniform continuity on a set strengthens it by choosing one input tolerance that works at every point:

\eqdisplay{\forall\epsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall x,y:\quad |x-y|<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x)-f(y)|<\epsilon.}

For $x^2$ on $[0,1]$, the bound $|x^2-y^2|\leq2|x-y|$ gives a uniform choice. On all of $\R$, no fixed $\delta$ works for a fixed small output tolerance, because $|x^2-y^2|=|x-y||x+y|$ grows with the location. The compact-interval theorem stated earlier guarantees uniform continuity for every continuous function on $[a,b]$. That common control will allow the errors from many integration subintervals to be bounded at once.

\FloatBarrier
\section{The derivative as a local linear model}

\subsection{Difference quotients and the remainder}

Fix an interior point $a$ of the domain. The difference quotient is the slope between two distinct points of the graph. If its limit is finite, that limit defines the derivative:

\eqdisplay{f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}h.}

The quotient is evaluated for $h\ne0$. Its limit does not arise by substituting zero into a zero denominator. Multiplying the defining error by $h$ gives an equivalent statement:

\eqdisplay{f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+r(h),\qquad \frac{r(h)}h\to0.}

This is the local linear model. The graph differs from its tangent line by an amount small compared with $|h|$. Requiring only $r(h)\to0$ would give continuity, not differentiability. A corner such as $|x|$ has a small change in value but no single linear coefficient that works on both sides.

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness of the linear model and continuity]
If $f$ is differentiable at an interior point $a$, its local linear coefficient is unique and $f$ is continuous at $a$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If both $A$ and $B$ gave remainders of order $o(h)$, subtracting the two representations and dividing by $h$ would give $A-B\to0$. Since $A-B$ is constant, it must be zero. Differentiability also implies continuity because both $f'(a)h$ and $r(h)$ tend to zero.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Two elementary calculations}

\begin{example}[Square and reciprocal]
For the square function, expansion is exact:

\eqdisplay{(a+h)^2-a^2=2ah+h^2,\qquad \frac{(a+h)^2-a^2}h=2a+h\to2a.}

Its linearisation is $a^2+2ah$, and its remainder is $h^2$. For $f(x)=1/x$ with $a\ne0$,

\eqdisplay{\frac{1/(a+h)-1/a}h=-\frac1{a(a+h)}\to-\frac1{a^2}.}

The denominator stays nonzero for sufficiently small $h$. Both computations use an algebraic simplification valid away from $h=0$, followed by a limit. Neither discards a nonzero term without explaining why its contribution tends to zero.
\end{example}

If $x$ has dimensions of time and $f$ of distance, the derivative has dimensions of speed. A second derivative has dimensions of acceleration. In a purely mathematical graph, the same construction measures sensitivity without requiring a physical motion.

\subsection{A derivative need not be continuous}

The left and right difference quotients of $|x|$ at zero are $-1$ and 1, so the derivative fails there. A different obstruction appears for

\eqdisplay{f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}x^2\sin(1/x),&x\ne0,\\0,&x=0.\end{array}\right.}

At zero, the quotient is $h\sin(1/h)$, which tends to zero by squeezing. Thus $f'(0)=0$. At nonzero $x$, the rules established in the next section give

\eqdisplay{f'(x)=2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x).}

This derivative does not tend to zero at zero. The original function is differentiable everywhere, but its derivative is discontinuous. Requiring a continuous derivative is an additional hypothesis, often useful for estimates, rather than part of the definition of a derivative.

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calc-02-differentiability.pdf}
\caption{Calculated regularity examples. Left: $|x|$ is continuous but has unequal one-sided slopes at zero. Right: the derivative of the oscillatory function in the text, with $f'(0)=0$ marked. Finite sampling cannot display every oscillation near zero; the formula and the sequence argument determine its limiting behaviour.}\label{fig:regularity}
\end{figure}

For instance, at $x_n=1/(2\pi n)$ the derivative equals $-1$, while at $y_n=1/((2n+1)\pi)$ it equals 1. Both sequences approach zero. The two incompatible limiting values prove the derivative's discontinuity independently of the displayed graph.

\FloatBarrier
\section{Rules for differentiating functions}

\subsection{Sums, products and quotients}

The linear model provides the differentiation rules without treating the derivative as an isolated list of formulas. If $u$ and $v$ are differentiable at $a$, write their increments as $u'(a)h+o(h)$ and $v'(a)h+o(h)$. Adding the models or multiplying them by a constant gives the sum and scaling rules.

For a product, an exact identity separates the first-order increments from their interaction:

\eqdisplay{\Delta(uv)=u\,\Delta v+v\,\Delta u+\Delta u\,\Delta v.}

Both increments are $O(h)$, so their product is $O(h^2)$ and becomes zero after division by $h$ and passage to the limit. Therefore

\eqdisplay{(u+v)'=u'+v',\qquad (cu)'=cu',\qquad (uv)'=u'v+uv'.}

For a reciprocal, the same difference-quotient calculation used for $1/x$ gives $(1/v)'=-v'/v^2$ where $v\ne0$. Combining it with the product rule yields

\eqdisplay{\left(\frac uv\right)'=\frac{u'v-uv'}{v^2},\qquad v\ne0.}

The denominator condition belongs to the rule. A cancellation in a simplified expression may permit an extension to a missing point, but that is a separate function and must be defined there.

\subsection{Composition and the chain rule}

\begin{theorem}[Chain rule]\label{thm:chain}
If $g$ is differentiable at $a$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(a)$, their composition is differentiable at $a$ with derivative $f'(g(a))g'(a)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $k=g(a+h)-g(a)$. Differentiability of $g$ gives $k=g'(a)h+o(h)$, so $k=O(h)$. The outer function has the model

\eqdisplay{f(g(a)+k)=f(g(a))+f'(g(a))k+k\rho(k),\qquad \rho(k)\to0.}

Define $\rho(0)=0$ if necessary. This keeps the formula valid even for increments at which $g(a+h)=g(a)$. Substituting the model for $k$, the final term divided by $h$ is $(k/h)\rho(k)\to0$. It follows that

\eqdisplay{(f\circ g)'(a)=f'(g(a))g'(a).}
\end{proof}

This argument avoids dividing by the intermediate change $k$, which may vanish for nonzero $h$. The inner derivative measures how the intermediate variable changes; the outer derivative measures sensitivity to that intermediate variable. Their product measures the complete first-order response.

\begin{example}[A composed power]
For example, $(1+x^2)^5$ has derivative $10x(1+x^2)^4$. The power rule applies to the outer function while $2x$ accounts for the inner change. Treating the entire expression as a fifth power of $x$ would omit that dependence.
\end{example}

\subsection{Powers and circular functions}

For a positive integer $n$, the binomial expansion gives $(x+h)^n-x^n=nx^{n-1}h+O(h^2)$. Division by $h$ proves the power rule. Negative integer powers follow from reciprocals, and rational powers follow on intervals where the corresponding real branch is defined. A later construction using logarithms extends the rule to arbitrary real powers of positive $x$.

\eqdisplay{\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}.}

The sine derivative depends on the radian normalization. Elementary unit-circle geometry gives, for $0<h<\pi/2$, $\sin h<h<\tan h$. Dividing by $\sin h$ and squeezing gives $\sin h/h\to1$. Symmetry supplies the negative approach. Also,

\eqdisplay{\frac{1-\cos h}{h}=\frac{\sin^2h}{h(1+\cos h)}\to0.}

The angle-addition identities then reduce the sine and cosine difference quotients to these two limits:

\eqdisplay{(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad (\cos x)'=-\sin x,\qquad (\tan x)'=\frac1{\cos^2x}.}

The last formula applies where $\cos x\ne0$. If a numerical angle were expressed in degrees, differentiating with respect to that degree coordinate would introduce a factor $\pi/180$. Radians make the geometric and analytic normalization agree.

\subsection{Inverse functions and implicit relations}

A continuous strictly monotone function on an interval has a continuous inverse on its image. Suppose $f'(a)\ne0$. Nearby inverse difference quotients are reciprocals of the corresponding nonzero quotients of $f$, so

\eqdisplay{(f^{-1})'(f(a))=\frac1{f'(a)}.}

The continuity of the inverse ensures that approaching $f(a)$ corresponds to approaching $a$. The formula is not a proof that an arbitrary function has an inverse. Restricting sine to $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ gives the inverse branch $\arcsin$. At its interior points,

\eqdisplay{(\arcsin x)'=\frac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}},\quad |x|<1;\qquad (\arctan x)'=\frac1{1+x^2}.}

An equation can instead describe a branch implicitly. On a differentiable branch of $x^2+y^2=R^2$, regard $y$ as a function of $x$ and differentiate both sides:

\eqdisplay{2x+2y\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=0,\qquad \frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-\frac xy\quad(y\ne0).}

At the circle's leftmost and rightmost points, $y=0$ and the tangent is vertical. The failure of a finite derivative with respect to $x$ there does not mean that the geometric curve has a corner. It means that this local graph coordinate is unsuitable for a finite slope.

\FloatBarrier
\section{From local slopes to finite change}

\subsection{An interior extremum}

\begin{theorem}[Fermat's stationary-point condition]
If a differentiable function has a local extremum at an interior point $c$, then $f'(c)=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $f$ has a local maximum at $c$. For small positive $h$, the quotient $[f(c+h)-f(c)]/h$ is nonpositive. For negative $h$, it is nonnegative. A common finite limit must therefore be zero. The minimum case follows by changing signs.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Stationarity is a necessary condition]
A zero derivative is necessary at a differentiable interior extremum, not sufficient. The function $x^3$ has derivative zero at zero and is increasing through it. Endpoints and nondifferentiable points must also be examined in an optimisation problem.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Rolle's theorem and the Mean Value Theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Rolle's theorem]\label{thm:rolle}
Let $a<b$. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f(a)=f(b)$, there is a point $c\in(a,b)$ with $f'(c)=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The extreme-value theorem supplies a maximum and minimum. If the function is not constant, at least one extremum occurs in the interior. Fermat's condition gives $f'(c)=0$ there. If the function is constant, any interior point works.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Mean Value Theorem]\label{thm:mvt}
Let $a<b$. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, there is a point $c\in(a,b)$ such that

\eqdisplay{f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Subtract the line joining $(a,f(a))$ and $(b,f(b))$. The resulting function is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and has equal endpoint values. Rolle's theorem gives a point where its derivative is zero, which is the asserted identity.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem]
Continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on its interior are both required. Applying the conclusion to $|x|$ on $[-1,1]$ would ask for derivative zero somewhere, although every existing derivative there is $-1$ or 1. The missing derivative at zero is exactly the failed hypothesis.
\end{remark}

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calc-03-mean-value-optimization.pdf}
\caption{Calculated applications of derivative information. Left: the chord of $x^2$ on $[0,2]$ is parallel to the tangent at 1, as the Mean Value Theorem predicts. Right: the volume function for the open-box construction in the text. The endpoint comparison establishes the displayed maximum.}\label{fig:mvt}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Monotonicity and a bound on error}

If $f'>0$ throughout an interval, applying the theorem between any two distinct points proves that $f$ is strictly increasing. If $f'\geq0$, the conclusion is nondecreasing. If $f'=0$ everywhere on an interval, any two function values agree, so $f$ is constant there. This last conclusion explains why antiderivatives of one function differ only by a constant on a connected interval.

The theorem also turns a derivative bound into a finite-change bound. If $|f'|\leq K$ between two points and the endpoint continuity hypotheses hold, then

\eqdisplay{|f(b)-f(a)|\leq K|b-a|.}

This is a Lipschitz estimate. Unlike a statement about one tangent, it controls an entire interval. A large derivative can amplify input error; a small derivative bound limits the amplification. The estimate supplies a mathematical reason to inspect the domain over which an approximation will be used.

\subsection{Concavity and the shape of a graph}

If $f''>0$ on an interval, the first derivative is increasing there. The graph is concave upward: its slopes increase as the input increases. The Mean Value Theorem then places the graph above each tangent within that interval. For $f''<0$, the slopes decrease and the graph lies below its tangents. An inflection point requires a change of concavity. A zero second derivative alone is insufficient; $x^4$ has $f''(0)=0$ while remaining concave upward on both sides.

A curve sketch can therefore combine distinct pieces of information: the domain and its excluded points, intercepts, limits near boundaries and at infinity, signs of $f'$ and $f''$, and values at critical points. A finite plot may hide a narrow feature or a vertical asymptote. For $1/x$, neither an apparent connecting line across zero nor an arbitrary plotting cutoff belongs to the function. The limiting and derivative information determines which features a faithful sketch must retain.

\subsection{Optimisation and related rates}

\begin{example}[The maximum-volume open box]
Cut squares of side $x$ from the corners of a square sheet of side 12 and fold the remaining edges upward. In consistent length units the volume is $V=x(12-2x)^2$, with physical range $0\leq x\leq6$. Its derivative is

\eqdisplay{V'(x)=(12-2x)(12-6x).}

The only interior stationary point is $x=2$. The derivative is positive before it and negative afterwards. The endpoint volumes vanish, so $V(2)=128$ is the global maximum on the stated interval. The domain restriction prevents an algebraic continuation with negative side lengths from entering the physical comparison.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[An expanding sphere]
For related rates, the relation between quantities is differentiated before numerical values are inserted. A sphere with radius $r(t)$ has volume $V(t)=4\pi r(t)^3/3$, hence

\eqdisplay{\frac{\mathrm dV}{\mathrm dt}=4\pi r^2\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm dt}.}

At $r=2$ length units and $\mathrm dr/\mathrm dt=3$ length units per time unit, the rate is $48\pi$ volume units per time unit. Replacing $r$ by its instantaneous value before differentiating would turn a changing quantity into a constant and lose the rate being sought.
\end{example}

\FloatBarrier
\section{Linear approximation and Newton iteration}

\subsection{The size of a neglected term}

The approximation $f(a+h)\simeq f(a)+f'(a)h$ becomes informative only when its remainder is controlled over the required range. For $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ at $a=4$, it gives $\sqrt{4+h}\simeq2+h/4$. The derivative exists only for positive arguments, and the approximation is local. Taylor's theorem later gives a quantitative second-order remainder.

At an extremum a first-order model may be constant, so second-order information becomes decisive. If $f$ has a continuous second derivative near $c$ and $f'(c)=0$, then

\eqdisplay{f(c+h)-f(c)=\frac12 f''(c)h^2+o(h^2).}

Thus $f''(c)>0$ gives a strict local minimum, while $f''(c)<0$ gives a strict local maximum. When the second derivative is zero, the test is inconclusive. The functions $x^4$, $-x^4$ and $x^3$ show all three possible behaviours at zero.

\subsection{Turning the tangent into a root estimate}

Suppose a current estimate $x_n$ is near a zero of $f$. Replace the graph by its tangent at $x_n$ and find where that line meets the horizontal axis. Solving $0=f(x_n)+f'(x_n)(x_{n+1}-x_n)$ gives

\eqdisplay{x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)},\qquad f'(x_n)\ne0.}\label{eq:newton-placeholder}

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=.58\textwidth]{calc-newton-iteration.pdf}
\caption{Newton's tangent construction. The current point $(x_n,f(x_n))$ determines a tangent whose horizontal intercept is $x_{n+1}$. Vector illustration by Oleg Alexandrov, redrawn by Pbroks13 with later labels by Shubjt, via Wikimedia Commons; public domain. The drawing is schematic, not a computed trajectory for a specified function.}\label{fig:newton}
\end{figure}

\begin{example}[Newton iteration for the square root of two]
For $f(x)=x^2-2$, the update becomes $(x_n+2/x_n)/2$. From $x_0=1$, its first values are $1.5$, $1.416666\ldots$ and $1.414215686\ldots$. For any positive starting value the first update is at least $\sqrt2$, because

\eqdisplay{\frac12\left(x+\frac2x\right)-\sqrt2=\frac{(x-\sqrt2)^2}{2x}\geq0.}

Above $\sqrt2$ the update is smaller than $x$ while remaining above the root. Completeness therefore supplies a limit, and the fixed-point equation identifies it as $\sqrt2$. The exact error equation is

\eqdisplay{e_{n+1}=\frac{e_n^2}{2x_n},\qquad e_n=x_n-\sqrt2.}

Once the error is small, squaring it explains the rapid gain in accuracy. This is an exact relation in real arithmetic. Floating-point rounding eventually limits the computed improvement.
\end{example}

\subsection{Local convergence and global failure}

For a general simple root $\alpha$, assume $f$ is twice continuously differentiable nearby and $f'(\alpha)\ne0$. Taylor's theorem applied between $x_n$ and $\alpha$ gives

\eqdisplay{e_{n+1}=\frac{f''(\xi_n)}{2f'(x_n)}e_n^2,}

where $\xi_n$ lies between them. In a sufficiently small neighbourhood, $|f'|\geq m>0$ and $|f''|\leq M$. Then $|e_{n+1}|\leq M|e_n|^2/(2m)$. Choosing the initial error small enough keeps the iterates in the neighbourhood and makes the errors tend to zero at least quadratically. If the leading coefficient vanishes, convergence can be faster.

These local hypotheses do not guarantee convergence from every starting point. A horizontal tangent makes the update undefined. For $f(x)=x^3-2x+2$, starting at zero gives the exact cycle $0,1,0,1,\ldots$. For a root of multiplicity $m>1$, the model $f(x)=(x-\alpha)^m$ instead gives $e_{n+1}=(1-1/m)e_n$, which is only linear convergence. The optional basin picture in \ref{sec:basins} explores how global dependence on the starting point can remain complicated even when each root is locally attracting.

\FloatBarrier
\section{The definite integral as a controlled sum}

\subsection{Partitions, tags and mesh}

Let $f$ be bounded on $[a,b]$, where $a<b$. A partition consists of points $a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$. Choose a tag $\xi_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$ in each subinterval. Its Riemann sum is

\eqdisplay{S(f,P,\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^nf(\xi_i)\Delta x_i,\qquad \Delta x_i=x_i-x_{i-1},\qquad \|P\|=\max_i\Delta x_i.}

The mesh $\|P\|$ measures the largest remaining interval. Merely increasing the number of intervals is insufficient if one interval remains large. The Riemann integral is $I$ if every sufficiently fine tagged partition has its sum close to $I$:

\eqdisplay{\forall\epsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0:\quad \|P\|<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ |S(f,P,\xi)-I|<\epsilon\quad\hbox{for all tags}.}

The requirement covers arbitrary partitions, not only one selected sequence of equal subdivisions or one convenient set of sample points. This is how the definition prevents the sampling choice from deciding the answer.

\subsection{Lower and upper sums}

Let $m_i$ and $M_i$ be the infimum and supremum of $f$ on the $i$th subinterval. Then every tagged sum lies between

\eqdisplay{L(f,P)=\sum_i m_i\Delta x_i,\qquad U(f,P)=\sum_i M_i\Delta x_i.}

Refining a partition raises its lower sum and lowers its upper sum. Completeness supplies the supremum of all lower sums and the infimum of all upper sums. They agree precisely when the bounded function is Riemann integrable. Equivalently, for every $\epsilon>0$ there is a partition for which $U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\epsilon$. This is the Darboux criterion, used here in its equivalent form of the Riemann definition.

\begin{theorem}[Continuous functions are Riemann integrable]\label{thm:integrable}
Every continuous real-valued function on a closed bounded interval $[a,b]$, with $a<b$, is Riemann integrable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The extreme-value theorem gives boundedness. Uniform continuity ensures that every sufficiently short subinterval has oscillation smaller than $\epsilon/(b-a)$. Consequently,

\eqdisplay{U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\Delta x_i<\frac{\epsilon}{b-a}\sum_i\Delta x_i=\epsilon.}

Thus every continuous function on a closed bounded interval is Riemann integrable. The crucial step is that one interval length works everywhere, allowing all the small errors to be controlled together.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A limit that can be computed directly}

\begin{example}[Integrating a square directly from sums]
For $x^2$ on $[0,1]$, equal subintervals give a lower sum using left endpoints and an upper sum using right endpoints. The finite sum-of-squares identity gives

\eqdisplay{L_n=\frac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6n^3},\qquad U_n=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n^3},\qquad U_n-L_n=\frac1n.}

Both sums tend to $1/3$, so their common value is the integral. The exact gap $1/n$ quantifies the bracketing error. The answer has not been obtained by presuming an antiderivative formula before integration is defined.
\end{example}

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calc-04-riemann.pdf}
\caption{Calculated lower and upper sums for $x^2$ on $[0,1]$. Shaded rectangles use left endpoints, and red top edges mark the upper rectangles. Increasing the subdivision count narrows the exact upper--lower gap from $1/4$ to $1/12$.}\label{fig:riemann}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Integrability is a real condition}

\begin{example}[A bounded function that is not Riemann integrable]
Define $D(x)=1$ for rational $x$ and $D(x)=0$ for irrational $x$ on $[0,1]$. Every nontrivial interval contains both kinds of number. Every lower sum is zero and every upper sum is one. The function is bounded but fails the Darboux criterion. Sampling only rational or only irrational tags would produce incompatible answers.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[Integrable discontinuities]
By contrast, changing a bounded integrable function at finitely many points does not change its integral. Those points can be covered by intervals of arbitrarily small total length, and the additional upper--lower contribution is bounded by that length times a fixed height bound. A finite jump can therefore be compatible with integrability. Continuity is sufficient, but it is not necessary.
\end{remark}

For nonnegative $f$, the integral agrees with the area under the graph. In general it is signed accumulation. Reversing endpoints changes the sign, and additivity and linearity follow by combining the corresponding sums:

\eqdisplay{\int_a^b f\dd x=-\int_b^a f\dd x,\qquad \int_a^c f\dd x+\int_c^b f\dd x=\int_a^b f\dd x.}

The symbol $x$ in a definite integral is a bound variable. Replacing it consistently by $t$ changes no value. An indefinite integral, by contrast, denotes a family of antiderivatives. Their relationship is the subject of the next section.

\FloatBarrier
\section{The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus}

\subsection{Differentiating an accumulation function}

\begin{theorem}[Fundamental Theorem: differentiation of accumulation]\label{thm:ftc-one}
Let $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, with $a<b$, and put $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\dd t$. Then $F$ is differentiable at every interior point and $F'(x)=f(x)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For an interior point $x$ and a small nonzero $h$, additivity gives

\eqdisplay{\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}h-f(x)=\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}[f(t)-f(x)]\dd t.}

For either sign of $h$, the absolute value is at most the largest value of $|f(t)-f(x)|$ between the two endpoints. Continuity makes that bound tend to zero. Therefore

\eqdisplay{\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\int_a^x f(t)\dd t=f(x).}
\end{proof}

The accumulation function has a derivative even if no elementary expression for the integral is known. For instance, $\int_0^x e^{-t^2}\dd t$ will define a valid differentiable function once the exponential is constructed. An elementary antiderivative is a matter of available notation, not a prerequisite for existence.

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calc-05-fundamental-theorem.pdf}
\caption{Calculated accumulation example for $f(t)=t^2$. Left: increasing the upper endpoint from 1 to 1.2 adds the shaded strip. Its displayed width is finite; the derivative argument takes a limit as the width tends to zero. Right: $F(x)=x^3/3$ and its derivative.}\label{fig:ftc}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Evaluating an integral from any antiderivative}

\begin{theorem}[Fundamental Theorem: endpoint evaluation]\label{thm:ftc-two}
Let $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, with $a<b$. If $G$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $G'=f$ there, then

\eqdisplay{\int_a^b f(x)\dd x=G(b)-G(a).}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The accumulation function $F$ is continuous on $[a,b]$: boundedness of $f$ gives $|F(y)-F(x)|\leq K|y-x|$ for a bound $|f|\leq K$. Theorem~\ref{thm:ftc-one} gives $F'=f$ on the interior. The Mean Value Theorem then makes $G-F$ constant on $[a,b]$. Since $F(a)=0$, comparing its endpoint values proves the formula.
\end{proof}

This endpoint formula is the evaluation form of the Fundamental Theorem. The proof joins three ingredients that were previously distinct: existence of the integral, differentiation of accumulation, and constancy of a function whose derivative is zero. The numbering of the theorem's two forms varies among textbooks; their content is what matters here.

For $x^2$, the antiderivative $x^3/3$ reproduces the value $1/3$ previously obtained from sums. In general, finding an antiderivative makes evaluation efficient, but it does not replace checking that the integral's interval and singularities satisfy the hypotheses.

\subsection{Variable endpoints and a net change}

If $u$ and $v$ are differentiable and $f$ is continuous on the required range, the chain rule gives

\eqdisplay{\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f(t)\dd t=f(v(x))v'(x)-f(u(x))u'(x).}

\begin{example}[Two moving endpoints]
For example, differentiating $\int_{x^2}^{\sin x}(1+t^2)\dd t$ gives $(1+\sin^2x)\cos x-2x(1+x^4)$. Both moving endpoints contribute.
\end{example} The integrand here depends on its integration variable alone; differentiating an additional parameter inside the integrand would require a further theorem.

\begin{remark}[Net change and total accumulation]
The same endpoint relation turns a rate into a net change. If $s'=v$ and the hypotheses hold, then $s(b)-s(a)=\int_a^b v(t)\dd t$. Total distance is instead $\int_a^b|v(t)|\dd t$. A reversal of direction can cancel displacement while still contributing positive distance.
\end{remark}
