\includegraphics[width=.52\textwidth]{calc-integral-region.pdf}
\caption{Geometric interpretation of a definite integral for a nonnegative function. The shaded region has area $S=\int_a^b f(x)\dd x$. Vector artwork by 4C, with revisions by Oleg Alexandrov and Antonsusi, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. No specific formula for the schematic curve is asserted.}\label{fig:integral-region}
\end{figure}

\FloatBarrier
\section{Logarithms, exponentials and differential equations}

\subsection{A function defined by its accumulation}

The Fundamental Theorem permits a construction of the logarithm that does not assume its derivative in advance. For $x>0$, define

\eqdisplay{\ln x=\int_1^x\frac1t\dd t,\qquad (\ln x)'=\frac1x.}

The derivative is positive, so the logarithm is strictly increasing. To obtain its multiplication law, fix $a>0$ and differentiate $\ln(ax)-\ln x$. The derivative vanishes. Evaluating the constant at $x=1$ gives

\eqdisplay{\ln(ax)=\ln a+\ln x,\qquad \ln1=0,\qquad \ln(1/x)=-\ln x.}

Since $\ln2>0$, the values $\ln(2^n)=n\ln2$ are unbounded above. The reciprocal identity supplies unbounded negative values. Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem show that the logarithm maps $(0,\infty)$ onto $\R$.

\subsection{The exponential as the inverse}

Define $E$ to be the inverse of the logarithm. The inverse derivative rule gives $E'(x)=E(x)$ and $E(0)=1$. The multiplication identity becomes $E(s+t)=E(s)E(t)$. Write $e=E(1)$ and use $e^x$ for $E(x)$. This notation is consistent with integer powers through the addition law.

For $a>0$, define $a^x=e^{x\ln a}$. The chain rule now establishes the general exponential and positive-base power rules:

\eqdisplay{\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}a^x=a^x\ln a,\qquad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}x^p=px^{p-1}\quad(x>0,\ p\in\R).}

The real-power restriction avoids assuming that a negative number has every real power. Special integer or rational exponents can have larger real domains, but those domains must be specified separately.

The derivative of $\ln|x|$ is $1/x$ on either side of zero. Consequently, $\int 1/x\dd x=\ln|x|+C$ on any interval avoiding zero. There can be different constants on the two disconnected intervals. An antiderivative expression does not bridge the singularity.

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calc-06-logarithm-exponential.pdf}
\caption{Calculated logarithm and exponential relations. Left: inverse graphs reflected in $y=x$. Right: two exact solutions of $y'=-y$, selected by different initial values. These curves represent stated mathematical models, not fitted observations.}\label{fig:log-exp}
\end{figure}

\subsection{A rate law and its initial condition}

For constant $k$, the equation $y'=ky$ says that the instantaneous rate is proportional to the current value. The product rule gives $(ye^{-kt})'=0$. Thus every differentiable solution on an interval containing zero is

\eqdisplay{y(t)=y_0e^{kt},\qquad y(0)=y_0.}

This proof includes $y_0=0$ without dividing by $y$. A negative $k$ gives decay and a positive $k$ gives growth. The parameter has dimensions of inverse time if $t$ is a physical time. A rate law inferred from measurements would need an additional empirical justification; no such inference is being made here.

For a separable equation $y'=g(t)h(y)$, restrict first to a solution range where $h(y)\ne0$. Choose $H'(y)=1/h(y)$. The chain rule and endpoint integration give

\eqdisplay{H(y(t))-H(y(t_0))=\int_{t_0}^t g(s)\dd s.}

Zeros of $h$ must be checked separately as possible constant solutions. The algebraic separation does not itself prove existence or uniqueness for an arbitrary rate law. For example, on $t\geq0$, $y'=2\sqrt y$ with $y(0)=0$ admits both the zero solution and a solution that remains zero until a chosen time $a\geq0$, then equals $(t-a)^2$. Both satisfy the equation at the joining time. Additional hypotheses are needed for a general uniqueness theorem.

\FloatBarrier
\section{Methods of integration}

\subsection{Substitution and the transformed interval}

The chain rule can be reversed through the Fundamental Theorem. Let $f$ be continuous on a range containing $g([a,b])$ and let $g$ be continuously differentiable. If $F'=f$, then $(F\circ g)'=f(g)g'$. Endpoint evaluation proves

\eqdisplay{\int_a^b f(g(x))g'(x)\dd x=\int_{g(a)}^{g(b)}f(u)\dd u.}

The derivative factor describes how the integration variable changes. The endpoint changes describe the interval traversed by that variable. Both are needed. This oriented identity does not require $g$ to be one-to-one. If $g$ moves forward and backward through the same values, the signed contributions cancel accordingly. Rewriting an integral by an inverse branch is a different procedure and may require splitting the domain.

For instance, with $u=1+x^2$,

\eqdisplay{\int_0^1\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\dd x=\int_1^2\frac1u\dd u=\ln2.}

The relation $\mathrm du=2x\dd x$ is shorthand for the derivative factor in the proved substitution formula. It need not be justified by treating differentials as arbitrary independently cancellable real numbers.

\subsection{Integration by parts}

Integrate the product rule for continuously differentiable $u$ and $v$:

\eqdisplay{\int_a^b u(x)v'(x)\dd x=[u(x)v(x)]_a^b-\int_a^b u'(x)v(x)\dd x.}

This trades one integral for another. A useful choice simplifies one factor when differentiated while leaving an accessible antiderivative for the other. Taking $u=x$ and $v'=e^x$ gives $\int xe^x\dd x=xe^x-e^x+C$. Taking $u=\ln x$ and $v'=1$ gives $\int\ln x\dd x=x\ln x-x+C$ on $x>0$.

The boundary term is part of a definite calculation. It may contain the entire answer or determine whether an improper limit exists. Removing it because the new integrand looks simpler would change the identity.

\subsection{Trigonometric powers and substitution}

The choice of technique depends on the structure of the integrand. An odd sine power can retain one sine factor for substitution, using $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$. For example,

\eqdisplay{\int\sin^3x\dd x=-\cos x+\frac{\cos^3x}{3}+C.}

Even powers can use angle-doubling identities. Since $\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2$,

\eqdisplay{\int\sin^2x\dd x=\frac x2-\frac{\sin2x}{4}+C.}

A square root such as $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ suggests $x=a\sin\theta$ for $a>0$. Restricting $\theta$ to $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ makes $\cos\theta\geq0$, so the square root is $a\cos\theta$ rather than an unexamined signed expression. Integration gives

\eqdisplay{\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\dd x=\frac12\left[x\sqrt{a^2-x^2}+a^2\arcsin(x/a)\right]+C.}

The calculation applies on $(-a,a)$, with endpoint values available by continuity for the corresponding definite integral. The restriction is what makes the inverse substitution and square-root sign consistent.

\subsection{Rational functions and partial fractions}

A rational integrand is first divided if the numerator degree is at least the denominator degree. The proper fraction can then be decomposed according to real linear and irreducible quadratic factors, including all powers of repeated factors. The decomposition is an algebraic identity on the domain where the denominator is nonzero.

For a simple example,

\eqdisplay{\frac1{x^2-1}=\frac12\left(\frac1{x-1}-\frac1{x+1}\right),\qquad \int\frac{\mathrm dx}{x^2-1}=\frac12\ln\left|\frac{x-1}{x+1}\right|+C.}

Each connected interval excluding $\pm1$ has its own antiderivative constant. An irreducible quadratic instead produces logarithmic or inverse-tangent contributions. Completing the square gives

\eqdisplay{\int\frac{\mathrm dx}{x^2+2x+5}=\frac12\arctan\left(\frac{x+1}{2}\right)+C.}

These techniques organize broad families of integrals, but they do not guarantee that every continuous function has an elementary antiderivative. The definite-integral definition and numerical methods remain available when symbolic formulas do not close.

\FloatBarrier
\section{Geometric and weighted accumulation}

\subsection{Area and average value}

If continuous functions satisfy $f\geq g$ on $[a,b]$, the area between their graphs is $\int_a^b(f-g)\dd x$. If their order changes, split at the crossings or integrate $|f-g|$. The signed integral without this correction can cancel distinct positive areas.

For $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$, the order is fixed and

\eqdisplay{\mathcal A=\int_0^1(x-x^2)\dd x=\frac16.}

The average value of an integrable function on a nondegenerate interval is

\eqdisplay{f_{\rm av}=\frac1{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\dd x.}

For continuous $f$, its minimum and maximum bound the integral, so they also bound this average. The Intermediate Value Theorem supplies a point $c$ with $f(c)=f_{\rm av}$. This is the mean-value theorem for integrals. The normalization by interval length is essential; without it the integral is a total, with different units.

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calc-07-area-probability.pdf}
\caption{Calculated area and probability examples. Left: the region between $y=x$ and $y=x^2$ on $[0,1]$, with area $1/6$. Right: the normalized density $p(x)=2x$ on $[0,1]$. The shaded interval $x\geq1/2$ has probability $3/4$. The density is a chosen mathematical example, not an empirical distribution.}\label{fig:area-density}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Volumes from cross-sections}

Suppose a solid has cross-sectional area $A(x)$ perpendicular to the $x$-axis. Approximating short pieces by cylinders suggests $\sum A(\xi_i)\Delta x_i$. For the regular solids considered here, passage to the integral gives $V=\int_a^b A(x)\dd x$. The cross-section must represent the actual solid once, without overlapping or omitting pieces.

If $f\geq g\geq0$ and the region between them rotates about the $x$-axis, each cross-section is a washer. Rotating about the $y$-axis instead permits cylindrical shells when $x\geq0$:

\eqdisplay{V_x=\pi\int_a^b[f(x)^2-g(x)^2]\dd x,\qquad V_y=2\pi\int_a^b x[f(x)-g(x)]\dd x.}

The two expressions describe different solids. For the preceding region between $x$ and $x^2$, they give $V_x=2\pi/15$ and $V_y=\pi/6$. A radius is a distance from the chosen axis. Rotating a region that crosses the axis requires a fresh cross-section analysis rather than inserting signed radii into a memorized formula.

\subsection{Mass, work and probability}

For a rod with nonnegative linear density $\lambda(x)$, its mass is $M=\int_a^b\lambda(x)\dd x$. If $M>0$, the centre of mass is the weighted average

\eqdisplay{\bar x=\frac1M\int_a^b x\lambda(x)\dd x.}

The same weighted-sum structure appears in probability. A nonnegative density $p$ has total integral one, and its integral over an interval gives the probability assigned to that interval. For $p(x)=2x$ on $[0,1]$, the total is one, $P(X\geq1/2)=3/4$, and the mean is $\int_0^1xp(x)\dd x=2/3$. The density's value at a point is not itself the probability of that point; an interval width is still needed in the approximating sum.

A variable force supplies another accumulation. Along a line, work is $\int F(x)\dd x$. For a spring with restoring-force magnitude $kx$, quasistatic extension from 0 to $b$ requires external work $kb^2/2$. The integral adds the changing force over distance. Multiplying the final force by the full distance would double this value because the force was smaller during the earlier extension.

\FloatBarrier
\section{Parametric and polar curves}

\subsection{A curve need not be a single graph}

Represent a plane path by two functions of one parameter, $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t)$. This is still a one-variable calculation. Suppose the coordinate functions are continuously differentiable. Where $x'(t)\ne0$, the inverse and chain rules give the first relation below. The second requires twice differentiable coordinate functions:

\eqdisplay{\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)},\qquad \frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac1{x'(t)}\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}\right).}

If $x'=0$ and $y'\ne0$, the tangent is vertical. If both vanish, neither formula decides the geometry, and the local parameterization needs further analysis. Different parameters can traverse the same curve at different speeds, or trace it more than once.

For a continuously differentiable regular curve, polygonal length sums converge to

\eqdisplay{L=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\sqrt{x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2}\dd t.}

The integrand follows by applying the local linear model to both coordinate increments and using the Euclidean distance formula. Standard rectifiable-curve theory justifies the limiting length identity for the stated regularity; its full partition proof is not repeated here. An isolated zero speed at an endpoint can be handled by a limiting or piecewise argument.

\subsection{A cycloid and a surface of revolution}

One unit-radius cycloid arch is $x=t-\sin t$, $y=1-\cos t$ for $0\leq t\leq2\pi$. Its speed is

\eqdisplay{\sqrt{(1-\cos t)^2+\sin^2t}=2\sin(t/2),\qquad L=\int_0^{2\pi}2\sin(t/2)\dd t=8.}

The sine is nonnegative over this interval; extending the speed formula to other intervals would require its absolute value. The parameter speed vanishes at the cusped endpoints, while the interior is regular.

For a regular curve above the $x$-axis, rotation around that axis gives surface area

\eqdisplay{S=2\pi\int_{t_0}^{t_1}y(t)\sqrt{x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2}\dd t.}

The approximation uses short conical frusta, whose areas tend to circumference times arc length. The formula assumes the surface is counted once and $y\geq0$ is the radius. It concerns a surface area, whereas the preceding washer integral concerns an enclosed volume.

\subsection{Polar area and its traversal}

For $x=r(\theta)\cos\theta$ and $y=r(\theta)\sin\theta$, a short angular sector has area approximately $r^2\Delta\theta/2$. When a continuous nonnegative radial graph traces the intended region once over $[\alpha,\beta]$, the area is

\eqdisplay{\mathcal A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta r(\theta)^2\dd\theta.}

The factor $1/2$ comes from sector geometry in radians. A polar curve may loop, cross the origin or retrace a region, so the angular interval is part of the geometric specification. The integral can otherwise count area more than once.

For the cardioid $r=1+\cos\theta$ on $[0,2\pi]$, the radius is nonnegative and the enclosed region is traced once. Using the integral of $\cos^2\theta$ gives

\eqdisplay{\mathcal A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(1+\cos\theta)^2\dd\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}.}

For a continuously differentiable radius, differentiating the Cartesian coordinates gives the corresponding polar length formula

\eqdisplay{L=\int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{r(\theta)^2+r'(\theta)^2}\dd\theta.}

It follows because the cross terms cancel in $x'^2+y'^2$. Both polar area and length therefore remain one-variable integrals, although they encode different local geometric quantities.

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calc-08-parametric-polar.pdf}
\caption{Calculated non-Cartesian descriptions. Left: one unit-radius cycloid arch, of length 8. Right: the cardioid $r=1+\cos\theta$, whose enclosed area is $3\pi/2$. The axes have equal scale within each panel.}\label{fig:curves}
\end{figure}

\FloatBarrier
\section{Improper limits and singular integrands}

\subsection{An infinite endpoint is a new limit}

The ordinary Riemann definition uses a bounded function on a finite interval. An infinite interval requires an additional limit:

\eqdisplay{\int_a^\infty f(x)\dd x=\lim_{B\to\infty}\int_a^B f(x)\dd x,}

provided the finite integrals exist and this limit is finite. An unbounded integrand at a finite endpoint is treated similarly, for instance $\int_0^1f=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\int_\epsilon^1f$. Calling the expression an integral does not establish convergence.

For the power family, endpoint evaluation gives two distinct thresholds:

\eqdisplay{\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\dd x=\frac1{p-1}\quad(p>1),\qquad \int_0^1x^{-p}\dd x=\frac1{1-p}\quad(p<1).}

The first diverges for $p\leq1$ and the second for $p\geq1$. At $p=1$, the logarithm provides the divergent endpoint behaviour. A function can decay to zero and still accumulate an infinite total, as $1/x$ at infinity demonstrates. An unbounded function can have finite improper area, as $x^{-1/2}$ near zero demonstrates.

\subsection{Comparison and a singularity inside an interval}

If $0\leq f\leq g$ sufficiently far out and $\int g$ converges, the increasing truncated integrals of $f$ are bounded above. Completeness supplies their finite limit. Conversely, a divergent nonnegative lower comparison proves divergence of a larger integrand. A finite initial interval does not affect convergence of the tail.

\begin{remark}[Principal value is a different limit]
An interior singularity at $c$ requires two independently convergent one-sided integrals. For $1/x$ on $[-1,1]$, the left side tends to $-\infty$ and the right side to $+\infty$. The improper integral does not exist. Symmetric deletion instead gives

\eqdisplay{\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\left(\int_{-1}^{-\epsilon}\frac{\mathrm dx}{x}+\int_\epsilon^1\frac{\mathrm dx}{x}\right)=0.}

That is a Cauchy principal value. Its coordinated cancellation is a different limiting operation from two independent improper integrals. Endpoint antiderivative evaluation across zero would erase precisely this distinction.
\end{remark}

\subsection{L'Hospital's rule and its hypotheses}

For a one-sided $0/0$ limit, suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at the limiting endpoint with common value zero, differentiable on a punctured interval, and $g'\ne0$ there. If $f'/g'\to L$, the Cauchy Mean Value Theorem gives

\eqdisplay{\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac{f'(c_x)}{g'(c_x)}\to L,}

where $c_x$ lies between the endpoint and $x$. The Cauchy theorem itself follows by applying Rolle's theorem to a linear combination of $f$ and $g$ chosen to have equal endpoint values. The nonzero derivative condition makes $g$ strictly monotone locally and permits the division.

There is also an $\infty/\infty$ version under the corresponding differentiability, denominator and derivative-ratio hypotheses. That extension is used as an established limit theorem here. The rule does not mean that every quotient can be replaced by the quotient of its derivatives. For example, $\lim_{x\to0}(1+x)/1=1$ is an ordinary limit, whereas differentiating the denominator would create an undefined quotient.

With the exponential already constructed, two valid applications give

\eqdisplay{\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1}{x}=1,\qquad \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln x}{x}=0.}

The first relation also follows directly from the derivative of the exponential at zero. Using the rule to establish $\sin x/x\to1$ would be circular if the sine derivative had itself been derived from that limit. The order of the arguments therefore matters even when the final calculation is short.

\FloatBarrier
\section{Infinite series and convergence}

\subsection{A sum means a limit of partial sums}

For a sequence $(a_n)$, define $S_N=\sum_{n=1}^Na_n$. The series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n$ converges to $S$ when $S_N\to S$. A necessary condition is $a_n\to0$, because $a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$. It is not sufficient. Grouping the harmonic series into blocks gives

\eqdisplay{\sum_{n=2^{k-1}+1}^{2^k}\frac1n\geq 2^{k-1}\frac1{2^k}=\frac12.}

Each new block contributes at least one-half, so the partial sums are unbounded. Every individual term tends to zero, but the accumulated tail does not become small. The geometric series behaves differently because its tail has a vanishing explicit bound.

For a series with nonnegative terms, the partial sums are increasing. The series converges precisely when those sums are bounded above, by completeness. This gives a framework in which comparison tests are statements about bounds on finite sums, followed by a justified limit.

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calc-09-improper-series.pdf}
\caption{Calculated partial accumulation. Left: integrals of $x^{-p}$ from 1 to a finite endpoint $B$. Right: partial sums of $1/n$ and $1/n^2$. Every displayed curve is finite. The comparison and block arguments, rather than the finite plots, determine convergence or divergence.}\label{fig:infinite}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Comparison, ratios and roots}

If $0\leq a_n\leq b_n$ eventually and $\sum b_n$ converges, the partial sums of $a_n$ are bounded and therefore converge. A divergent smaller nonnegative series proves divergence of a larger one. If $a_n/b_n\to c$ with $0<c<\infty$, eventual two-sided bounds give the limit-comparison test.

For decreasing positive $f$, rectangles compare $\sum f(n)$ with $\int f(x)\dd x$. The integral test applied to $f(x)=x^{-p}$ gives convergence of $\sum n^{-p}$ exactly when $p>1$. For $p\leq0$, even the term condition fails. When $p=2$, the omitted tail obeys

\eqdisplay{\frac1{N+1}\leq\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty\frac1{n^2}\leq\frac1N.}

This estimates an error without requiring a closed form for the full sum.

If the terms are eventually nonzero and $|a_{n+1}/a_n|\to q<1$, choose $q<r<1$. Every sufficiently late ratio is at most $r$, so the absolute tail is bounded by a geometric series. The series converges absolutely. If the ratio limit exceeds one, the terms fail to approach zero. A ratio limit of one gives no decision: both $1/n$ and $1/n^2$ have that limit.

The root test compares $|a_n|^{1/n}$ with a geometric ratio. If its limit is less than one there is absolute convergence; if it is greater than one the terms do not tend to zero. The test remains valid with an upper limit, or $\limsup$, replacing the ordinary limit. Here $\limsup b_n=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sup_{n\geq N}b_n$, allowing extended values. The equality case one is again inconclusive.

\subsection{Absolute convergence and cancellation}

If $\sum|a_n|$ converges, then any tail of $\sum a_n$ is bounded in magnitude by the corresponding absolute tail. The partial sums are Cauchy and converge in $\R$. Such a series is absolutely convergent. A convergent series whose absolute series diverges is conditionally convergent.

For an alternating series $b_1-b_2+b_3-\cdots$ with $b_n\geq0$, $b_n$ nonincreasing and $b_n\to0$, the even partial sums rise and the odd partial sums fall. They bound one another, and their gap tends to zero. Completeness gives a common limit. The remainder after $N$ terms has magnitude at most $b_{N+1}$.

The alternating harmonic series is therefore convergent although the harmonic series of its absolute values diverges. Its value is $\ln2$. One way to verify the value is to integrate the finite identity

\eqdisplay{\frac1{1+t}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(-t)^k+\frac{(-t)^N}{1+t},\qquad 0\leq t\leq1.}

The remainder integral has magnitude at most $\int_0^1t^N\dd t=1/(N+1)$, which tends to zero. This argument identifies the limit without assuming that an infinite series may automatically be integrated term by term at an endpoint.

\subsection{Pointwise and uniform convergence}

A sequence of functions can converge at every fixed input while lacking a common error bound across an interval. For $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$, the pointwise limit is zero for $x<1$ and one at $x=1$. Each $f_n$ is continuous, while the limit is not. The convergence is not uniform.

Uniform convergence to $f$ means that the largest error tends to zero:

\eqdisplay{\sup_{x\in E}|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0.}

\begin{theorem}[Continuity under uniform convergence]
The uniform limit of continuous real-valued functions on a set $E\subseteq\R$ is continuous on $E$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
To prove continuity at $a\in E$, choose one sufficiently large $N$ so that both $|f-f_N|$ errors are small, then use continuity of $f_N$ to control the middle term in

\eqdisplay{|f(x)-f(a)|\leq|f(x)-f_N(x)|+|f_N(x)-f_N(a)|+|f_N(a)-f(a)|.}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Integration under uniform convergence]
If Riemann-integrable functions $f_n$ on $[a,b]$ converge uniformly to $f$, then $f$ is Riemann integrable and

\eqdisplay{\left|\int_a^b f_n\dd x-\int_a^b f\dd x\right|\leq(b-a)\sup_{[a,b]}|f_n-f|\to0.}

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Uniform closeness to a bounded $f_N$ makes $f$ bounded. The difference between its upper and lower sums is at most the corresponding gap for $f_N$ plus $2(b-a)\sup|f-f_N|$. First choose $N$ to make the uniform error small, then a partition to make the gap for $f_N$ small. The Darboux criterion gives integrability. Integrating the uniform absolute-error bound gives the displayed inequality and hence convergence of the integrals.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Uniform convergence does not justify differentiating]
Differentiation needs more. The functions $\sin(nx)/n$ tend uniformly to zero, but their derivatives $\cos(nx)$ do not tend to the derivative zero; at $x=0$ they are always one. A sufficient theorem assumes uniformly convergent continuous derivatives together with convergence of the function values at one point. The Fundamental Theorem then constructs the limiting function by integrating the limiting derivative. It is the derivative control, rather than the graph's small height alone, that supports the exchange.
\end{remark}

\FloatBarrier
\section{Taylor approximation and power series}\label{sec:taylor}

\subsection{Matching derivatives at one point}

A linear approximation matches the value and first derivative. A degree-$n$ Taylor polynomial matches the derivatives through order $n$ at a centre $a$:

\eqdisplay{T_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k.}

The factorial appears because differentiating $(x-a)^k$ exactly $k$ times produces $k!$, while lower-order derivatives of that term vanish at $a$. These coefficients are forced by the matching conditions. They are not chosen by a numerical fit over an interval.

Matching derivatives does not yet bound the difference away from $a$. Write $f(x)=T_n(x)+R_n(x)$ and retain the remainder until its behaviour has been established.

\subsection{Taylor's theorem with a remainder}

\begin{theorem}[Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder]\label{thm:taylor}
Let $n\geq0$ be an integer and let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an interval containing distinct points $a$ and $x$. For the degree-$n$ Taylor polynomial at $a$, there is a point $\xi$ strictly between $a$ and $x$ such that

\eqdisplay{R_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}.}

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose $C$ so that $\psi(t)=f(t)-T_n(t)-C(t-a)^{n+1}$ vanishes at $t=x$. At $a$, $\psi$ and its first $n$ derivatives vanish. Repeated application of Rolle's theorem yields $\psi^{(n+1)}(\xi)=0$. Since the Taylor polynomial has zero $(n+1)$st derivative, this identifies $C=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)/(n+1)!$ and proves the formula.
\end{proof}

If $|f^{(n+1)}|\leq M$ between the endpoints, the computable consequence is

\eqdisplay{|R_n(x)|\leq\frac{M|x-a|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.}

The point $\xi$ need not be known. A valid bound on the derivative over the whole intervening interval is enough. \begin{example}[A certified square-root estimate]
For $f(x)=\sqrt x$ near 4, $f''(x)=-1/(4x^{3/2})$. On $[4,4.04]$ its magnitude is at most $1/32$. Thus the linear estimate $2.01$ for $\sqrt{4.04}$ has error at most $(0.04)^2/64=0.000025$. The concavity shows that the estimate is above the exact value.
\end{example}

\subsection{When the infinite polynomial represents the function}

The Taylor series represents $f$ at $x$ only if $R_n(x)\to0$ as $n\to\infty$. For the exponential on a fixed finite interval, every derivative equals the exponential and is bounded by a constant independent of $n$. The factorial bound makes the remainder tend to zero. For sine and cosine, all derivative magnitudes are at most one. Therefore

\eqdisplay{e^x=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{x^k}{k!},\qquad \sin x=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^kx^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!},\qquad \cos x=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^kx^{2k}}{(2k)!}.}

These identities hold for every real $x$. The factorial denominator dominates any fixed power, which can be proved by a ratio comparison. For $\sin x$, using its degree-seven polynomial on $|x|\leq1$ and treating the vanishing eighth coefficient explicitly gives $|R|\leq1/9!$. A low-degree approximation thus comes with an interval and an error estimate.

The geometric identity yields $1/(1-x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty x^k$ for $|x|<1$. Integrating on any smaller closed interval, where the convergence is uniform, gives

\eqdisplay{\ln(1+x)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{k+1}x^k}{k}\quad(|x|<1).}

At $x=1$ the series converges to $\ln2$ by the separate remainder argument already given. At $x=-1$ it diverges. The radius alone does not decide either endpoint.

\subsection{The radius of convergence}

For a power series $\sum c_n(x-a)^n$, the root test gives radius

\eqdisplay{R=\frac1{\limsup_{n\to\infty}|c_n|^{1/n}},}

with the conventions $1/0=\infty$ and $1/\infty=0$. There is absolute convergence for $|x-a|<R$ and divergence for $|x-a|>R$. Each endpoint at distance $R$ must be tested independently.

On any closed interval $|x-a|\leq r<R$, absolute geometric majorants give uniform convergence. The differentiated series has the same radius, because the additional factor $n$ does not change the limiting $n$th-root growth rate. Uniform convergence of that derivative series on smaller intervals justifies termwise differentiation. Termwise integration follows from the earlier integral bound. These operations are controlled inside the radius, without a blanket permission to exchange arbitrary infinite operations.

\subsection{Smoothness is not analyticity}

\begin{example}[A smooth function not represented by its Taylor series]
Define $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=e^{-1/x^2}$ for $x\ne0$. Every derivative away from zero is the exponential times a polynomial in $1/x$. For every fixed nonnegative integer $m$,

\eqdisplay{\lim_{x\to0}|x|^{-m}e^{-1/x^2}=0.}

To verify the limit, put $u=1/x^2$ and compare $u^{m/2}$ with $e^u$; an integer power above $m/2$ is enough for repeated L'Hospital differentiation or a positive exponential-series bound. The exponential wins over every such fixed power.

Induction, using the derivative difference quotient at zero at each stage, now gives $f^{(k)}(0)=0$ for every $k$. Its Taylor series at zero is identically zero, although $f(x)>0$ whenever $x\ne0$. The function is smooth but not analytic at zero. Its complete derivative data at that point do not determine its values in a neighbourhood through a Taylor series. The missing information resides in the remainder.
\end{example}

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calc-10-taylor.pdf}
\caption{Calculated Taylor examples. Left: sine and its degree-three and degree-seven Taylor polynomials at zero. Right: the smooth function $e^{-1/x^2}$, extended by zero at the origin, and its identically zero Taylor polynomials there. Agreement of every derivative at one point does not by itself imply a local series representation.}\label{fig:taylor}
\end{figure}

\section{Numerical approximation and its error}

\subsection{Finite differences in finite arithmetic}

The derivative is a limit, while a computer evaluates a quotient at a finite increment. For a smooth function, Taylor expansion gives the forward and central approximations

\eqdisplay{D_h^+f(a)=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}h,\qquad D_h^0f(a)=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a-h)}{2h}.}

The forward truncation error is $O(h)$. Symmetry cancels its first-order contribution in the central formula, giving $O(h^2)$ when the third derivative is bounded nearby. Specifically, bounds $|f''|\leq M_2$ and $|f'''|\leq M_3$ give errors at most $M_2|h|/2$ and $M_3h^2/6$, respectively, under the corresponding Taylor hypotheses.

Floating-point arithmetic adds a different error. Subtracting nearby function values can remove leading digits; dividing the remaining rounding error by $h$ amplifies it. In the usual rounding model this contribution can scale like $\epsilon_{\rm mach}/|h|$ times a function-value scale. The model explains why reducing $h$ indefinitely need not improve the computed quotient. It is not a universal exact error formula for every function or implementation.

The accompanying calculation differentiates $\sin x$ at $x=1$, using 161 logarithmically spaced increments from $10^{-1}$ to $10^{-17}$ in NumPy binary64 arithmetic. Errors are compared with the computed value $\cos1$. Both the approximations and their reference value have finite arithmetic precision. The graph shows the expected initial truncation trend and eventual loss of accuracy. It is a numerical illustration of competing errors, not an experimental measurement or a proof about every computer.

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=.88\textwidth]{calc-11-differentiation-error.pdf}
\caption{Computed absolute errors for forward and central differences of $\sin x$ at 1. The horizontal variable is a finite increment, not an infinitesimal. The reference is the binary64 evaluation of $\cos1$. At very small increments, rounding and subtraction dominate the truncation improvement.}\label{fig:diff-error}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Quadrature rules and regularity}

For $n$ equal subintervals of width $h=(b-a)/n$, the midpoint and trapezoid approximations are

\eqdisplay{M_n=h\sum_{i=1}^nf\left(a+(i-\frac12)h\right),\qquad T_n=h\left[\frac{f(a)+f(b)}2+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}f(a+ih)\right].}

They approximate each short piece by a constant or a line. Taylor's theorem about each midpoint bounds the local midpoint error by $M_2h^3/24$; summing the errors gives the global estimate. Linear-interpolation error gives the corresponding trapezoid estimate:

\eqdisplay{|I-M_n|\leq\frac{M_2(b-a)^3}{24n^2},\qquad |I-T_n|\leq\frac{M_2(b-a)^3}{12n^2},\qquad |f''|\leq M_2.}

Composite Simpson quadrature integrates a quadratic interpolant across each pair of subintervals. With even $n$, its endpoint, odd-index and even-index weights are

\eqdisplay{S_n=\frac h3\left[f(a)+f(b)+4\sum_{j=1}^{n/2}f(a+(2j-1)h)+2\sum_{j=1}^{n/2-1}f(a+2jh)\right].}

Here the displayed sums simply select odd and even interior nodes. The classical interpolation error theorem gives

\eqdisplay{|I-S_n|\leq\frac{M_4(b-a)^5}{180n^4},\qquad |f^{(4)}|\leq M_4,}

for a function with continuous fourth derivative. This bound is used as an established quadrature theorem; its full interpolation remainder proof is not reproduced. The regularity assumption and even-subdivision condition are retained. A singular integrand cannot inherit fourth-order behaviour merely because Simpson weights were applied to it.

No uncertainty interval or physical observation is being assigned to them.

\FloatBarrier
\section{Conclusions and scope}

Calculus turns approximation into an exact statement by controlling what remains in a limit. Completeness supports the existence of suitable limiting values. Differentiability identifies a unique local linear coefficient, while the Mean Value Theorem connects that coefficient to finite changes under interval hypotheses. Riemann integration requires the total sampling error to disappear across all sufficiently fine partitions. The Fundamental Theorem links the derivative of accumulation to its integrand and makes endpoint evaluation possible.

The later methods inherit these conditions. Substitution follows the chain rule and must transform endpoints and derivative factors consistently. Geometric integrals depend on the region, axis and traversal being counted. Improper integrals introduce new endpoint limits, and infinite series require convergence of partial sums. A Taylor polynomial becomes a representation only after the remainder is shown to vanish. Smoothness alone does not supply that conclusion.

The computations illustrate the difference between a mathematical limit and a finite implementation. Small increments compete with rounding error. Quadrature orders appear under suitable smoothness. Newton iteration is locally accurate near a simple root while its global basins can be intricate. The recorded grids, arithmetic, stopping criteria and data make these illustrations reproducible without giving them the status of proofs.

The exposition assumes the ordered complete real field and explicitly states the compactness, quadrature and curve-length results it uses. It does not construct the real numbers or develop Lebesgue integration, global complex dynamics or multivariable calculus. Throughout, a formula remains usable only when its approximation and domain have been accounted for.

\appendix
\renewcommand{\thesubsection}{\Alph{section}.\arabic{subsection}}
\section{Advanced extension: Newton basins in the complex plane}\label{sec:basins}

This appendix goes beyond real single-variable calculus. It connects the local real iteration in Section~7 with a finite illustration of complex polynomial dynamics. None of its results is needed for the main development.

\subsection{The algebraic extension}

The real Newton update can select different roots from different starting values. To display that dependence for a cubic, extend the polynomial arithmetic to $z=x+iy$, where $i^2=-1$. The pair $(x,y)$ gives the horizontal and vertical coordinates in the complex plane, and $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. Multiplication and division use ordinary algebra together with $i^2=-1$.

For $p(z)=z^3-1$, the same polynomial differentiation rule gives $p'(z)=3z^2$. Its Newton map is

\eqdisplay{N(z)=z-\frac{z^3-1}{3z^2}=\frac13\left(2z+\frac1{z^2}\right),\qquad z\ne0.}

Factoring $(z-1)(z^2+z+1)$ gives three roots:

\eqdisplay{\alpha_0=1,\qquad \alpha_1=-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i,\qquad \alpha_2=-\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i.}

For each root, its basin of attraction is the set of starting points whose exact iterates are defined and converge to that root. The basin is defined through an infinite limiting behaviour. A finite image can only sample and approximate its membership.

\subsection{Why a simple root attracts nearby iterates}

Fix a root $\alpha$ and write $z=\alpha+e$. Because $\alpha^3=1$, a direct algebraic calculation gives

\eqdisplay{N(z)-\alpha=\frac{(z-\alpha)^2(2z+\alpha)}{3z^2}.}

Near $\alpha$, the denominator stays away from zero and the remaining factor stays bounded. The new error is therefore bounded by a constant times $|e|^2$. This is the complex polynomial counterpart of the local real error estimate. It uses no claim that a general real-variable proof automatically establishes every result of complex analysis.

The local estimate does not classify every remote starting point. The pole at zero interrupts the update, and points near a pole can be carried far away. Iterates may eventually return to a root's neighbourhood or remain unresolved within a finite computation. Such possibilities make the global geometry richer than three simple nearest-root regions.

\subsection{What the sampled image records}

Figure~\ref{fig:basins} uses a $2000\times1250$ grid, including endpoints, over $-1.8\leq\mathop{\rm Re}z\leq1.8$ and $-1.125\leq\mathop{\rm Im}z\leq1.125$. Each starting point is iterated in NumPy complex128 arithmetic for at most 60 updates. The calculation checks the initial value and the result after each update. It accepts convergence when $|z^3-1|\leq10^{-10}$ and labels the point by the nearest exact root.

The update is guarded when $|3z^2|\leq10^{-14}$. Unresolved or guarded points are black. Blue denotes the root 1, orange the root with positive imaginary part, and green its conjugate. Brightness decreases with the number of updates before acceptance. The even grid sizes do not sample zero itself; its undefined update remains an exact algebraic fact rather than a pixel classification in this run.

\begin{figure}[htbp]\centering
\includegraphics[width=.72\textwidth]{calc-newton-basins.pdf}
\caption{Computed Newton-basin image for $z^3-1$, using the window, grid, stopping tolerance and iteration cap stated in the text. Colour identifies the accepted root and brightness encodes update count. The raster retains all $2000\times1250$ computed pixels. This is a mathematical numerical illustration, not a photograph, an experimental dataset or a proof of the boundary's structure.}\label{fig:basins}
\end{figure}

In this run 2,499,998 starting pixels meet the residual criterion and two remain unresolved at the cap. No sampled point triggers the derivative guard. These are counts for this particular grid and arithmetic. They do not measure the areas of exact basins, certify every accepted orbit in exact arithmetic or prove that either unresolved orbit fails to converge.

The finely interwoven boundary is commonly called a Newton fractal. Its global dynamical theory lies outside this exposition. The computation separates local convergence from global behaviour. An update that squares a small error near a root can make the eventual root difficult to infer remotely. Greater resolution reveals further sampled detail, but no finite image proves structure at every scale.
